METR (short for Model Evaluation and Threat Research) found no evidence that the attackers accessed sensitive information in either incident, and the org said it investigated both with security experts. METR researchers worked with OpenAI to investigate how its agents hacked Hugging Face, and on Monday, it disclosed two of its own security snafus. “In March 2026, attackers stole an API key for inference on public models and consumed a substantial amount of credits,” the nonprofit disclosed in a Monday report. “In May 2026, we observed attackers systematically probing our publicly accessible infrastructure, including an unsuccessful attempt to access internal data via an inadvertently exposed endpoint.” From fail-open bug to model-credit theft The March incident involved a METR researcher who didn’t have access to sensitive information - including model data and credentials, as well as information about model architectures, training, and release dates. The researcher used agents running on a personal EC2 instance that was “intentionally” left publicly accessible behind Google authentication. The instance contained an API key for METR’s public models account. According to METR’s account, a “vibe-coded app” included a fail-open bug that disabled authentication, and this exposed the system to the public internet for several days. “We suspect that the attacker found the instance by looking through recently-registered websites (e.g. in certificate transparency lists) to find vibe-coded sites with high-signal keywords relating to LLMs or agents, for purposes of harvesting potentially exposed model provider API keys,” the AI research org wrote. Once the attacker found the app, they prompted an agent to reveal its model provider API key, then added an SSH key to maintain persistent access, and over the next three weeks used the stolen credentials to consume API credits on public models worth about $600,000. Luckily for METR, the unnamed model developer had given the credits to the nonprofit for free. How do you not notice the 'large illicit usage?' METR does answer the question on everyone’s mind in the report: Why its researchers didn’t notice the “large illicit usage?” There are several reasons for this. First, the model testing operation regularly runs evaluations that use a lot of tokens, and this means the organization is “very acclimated to getting lots of weird rate limit and API errors.” So the high usage didn’t look that out of the ordinary. Plus, since the tokens were free, METR didn’t accrue a large bill, and at the time there was no way to put a spending limit on keys like the one that was stolen. In response to the March incident, METR says it improved its security infrastructure, protocols, and review process, and will continue to invest in security. To this end, it also hired a security lead, and plans to add more security staff. Crims used agents to try to access frontier models The second incident happened in early May, when “METR became the target of a sustained external attack campaign.” After being “tipped off” that attackers who appeared financially motivated may have been trying to gain illicit access to frontier models, METR watched the intruders probe its publicly accessible infrastructure. They also used agents to find ways to gain initial access, including automated vulnerability discovery, credential stuffing against authentication providers, attempting OAuth token grants, scanning newly deployed services, and phishing attempts. At the same time, METR unintentionally “exposed a read-only SQL query mechanism via our public transcript viewer.” While queries were scoped to public data by default, a bug allowed access to unpublished evaluation data, and “some sensitive model data was accidentally included in this database.” However, there’s no evidence that the attacker found the exploit or accessed any non-public data, according to the model testing body. An independent bug hunter discovered the vulnerability and reported it to METR, which paid the researcher a bounty, and took the API offline. In response, METR says it now uses an isolated production environment for public-facing applications that is separate from its internal infrastructure.®
paragraphs: The model provider gave METR the credits for free. An actual customer would not have been so lucky

AI model testing organization METR has disclosed two attacks that happened earlier this year, including one in which an attacker stole an API key and spent three weeks consuming public-model credits worth about $600,000.

METR (short for Model Evaluation and Threat Research) found no evidence that the attackers accessed sensitive information in either incident, and the org said it investigated both with security experts.
METR researchers worked with OpenAI to investigate how its agents hacked Hugging Face , and on Monday, it disclosed two of its own security snafus.

“In March 2026, attackers stole an API key for inference on public models and consumed a substantial amount of credits,” the nonprofit disclosed in a Monday report . “In May 2026, we observed attackers systematically probing our publicly accessible infrastructure, including an unsuccessful attempt to access internal data via an inadvertently exposed endpoint.”

The March incident involved a METR researcher who didn’t have access to sensitive information - including model data and credentials, as well as information about model architectures, training, and release dates. The researcher used agents running on a personal EC2 instance that was “intentionally” left publicly accessible behind Google authentication. The instance contained an API key for METR’s public models account.

draft_context.source_title: Facilitating AI integration with simplicity at scale
draft_context.description: As companies scale, the technology supporting operations can become a liability just as quickly as it becomes an asset. Disconnected systems, site-specific tools, spreadsheets, and manual workarounds can create data silos that make it harder to spot problems early, coordinate responses, and make decisions with confidence. For Jabil, a global manufacturing company with more than 100 sites across more than 30 countries, the answer has been to make integration and simplification a priority. The company adopted a “simplify-first, then-innovate mindset,” says Harish Manohar, SAP IT director at Jabil, recognizing that adding new technologies without first reducing complexity risks creating more risk. The goal is to standardize processes, consolidate where possible, and establish a more consistent data backbone across the organization. “Any innovation without simplification is going to add more complexity,” Manohar says. That philosophy also changes how Jabil approaches modernization. “Any modernization or transformation should add measurable business value,” Manohar says. The company is focused on connecting processes end-to-end across its supply chain and creating a foundation that can scale consistently across regions. Integration comes first because, as Manohar puts it, “the backbone of any contemporary or modern organization is data.” Before organizations can optimize, automate, or apply AI, data needs to flow seamlessly across systems. But doing that across a global organization is hardly straightforward. Jabil’s more than 100 sites operate with different levels of process maturity, legacy systems, and localized workflows, while regulated businesses bring additional compliance requirements. As such, standardizing across different regions and business environments means changing processes and governance without disrupting the operations already in place. The value of that work extends beyond the technology to the people using it. Integrated workflows can offer employees shared visibility into data, reduce manual data reconciliation, and help them move from chasing information to acting on insights. For Jabil, the aim is also to improve real-time visibility into supply chain events, which can enable faster responses to disruptions and reduce operational risk. Looking to the future, that foundation could make AI and automation all the more useful and scalable. With trusted data and integrated systems in place, Jabil is exploring predictive supply chain insights, intelligent exception handling, and AI-driven planning and forecasting. To Manohar, the takeaway is clear: “Simplicity at scale is a very competitive advantage,” and technology investments must ultimately connect to business value and operational resilience. This episode of Business Lab is produced in partnership with SAP. Full Transcript: Megan Tatum: From MIT Technology Review, I’m Megan Tatum, and this is Business Lab, the show that helps business leaders make sense of new technologies coming out of the lab and into the marketplace. Our topic today is enterprise technology integration, and how the benefits of consolidating tools and systems across the supply chain help organizations operate more reliably at scale. When companies reduce tool sprawl and connect their systems more effectively, they gain earlier visibility, faster response, and greater resilience across production lines. My guest today is Harish Manohar, SAP IT Director at Jabil. Jabil has been on a journey to simplify its technology landscape by using SAP Integration Suite as the foundation to connect systems, retire fragmented tools, and enable more consistent operations globally. This podcast is produced in partnership with SAP. Welcome, Harish. Harish Manohar: Hello, Megan. Good morning. Megan: Thank you so much for being here, Harish. Just to start, if we could set some context, can you give us a quick overview of Jabil, the business and its overall transformation journey? Harish: All right. So, about Jabil. Jabil is a global manufacturing company headquartered in St. Petersburg, Florida, USA. We have about 60 years of experience offering comprehensive engineering, supply chain, and manufacturing solutions across different industries. We have a global footprint of about over 100 different sites across 30-plus countries, 140,000-plus employees. We are a trusted partner for more than 400 of the world’s top brands. That’s a little bit about Jabil. Megan: Fantastic. And a lot of scale there, as you’re referring to some of the stats there. As things have got more complex, where did disconnected tools and systems start to slow you down, and what ultimately drove you to make integration a really strategic priority? Harish: I talked about our global footprint across 100-plus sites. With a global footprint always comes complexity about site-specific tools. All of our sites have been in business for a long time, and over the period of years, they had their own tools for their own processes. It’s a little bit disconnected. When we are looking to scale, the first thing we wanted to start looking at is what is this mix of site-specific tools, manual workarounds, spreadsheet-based processes, legacy applications, whatnot? That’s a big technical debt that we have had over the last 25 years. That’s where we started, and that is what led Jabil to make integration a strategic priority because we had limited ability to see issues early across plants, across regions, which would help us to coordinate responses consistently, and also to be able to scale those responses consistently. This complexity created data silos, and in a way delayed robust decision-making. As the complexity increased globally, integration became extremely critical to a few things. It was critical to establishing a single trusted data backbone, which would directly enable faster coordinated responses across the network. We at Jabil, as part of our transformation journey, believe that having the right data at the right time fundamentally changes how we respond to disruptions, which is all about a manufacturing business. How we respond to disruptions. This is where we started our strategic priority towards having a integrated system that drove data consistency across our landscape. Megan: Fantastic. As you have outlined there, there was obviously a real commercial need for this, but how did you think about bringing in those new technologies without adding even more complexity to the mix? Harish: Great question. Whenever we talk about transformation, we talk about all these bleeding-edge technologies that are out there today when it comes to AI and data, cloud, et cetera. But it was very important for us to put a stake in the ground and say and adopt a simplify-first, then-innovate mindset. Because any innovation without simplification is going to add more complexity, just like you mentioned. For us, SAP is our core digital platform. We want to focus on bringing more processes into SAP as much as possible. That is easier said than done because we have been in business for a while, global company, so not all processes exist within SAP at this point in time. We are slowly trying to standardize those processes, and having them under one single source of data would help us scale faster in terms of having data silos. We don’t want data silos across different systems. This is where we started to introduce newer capabilities around SAP. From a cloud standpoint, we have been using SAP’s BTP and Integration Suite, which is proving to be the center stage of all integrations across Jabil. Well, it’s not there yet, but that is the direction that we want to pursue is we don’t want to have a slew of different integration platforms, rather try and see where Integration Suite fits best and where other smaller integration platforms would add more value. Similarly, we have adopted an API-driven, event-based integration approach. That is our best practice that we have put down because we don’t want to keep moving data from one place to the other. That’s not good business practice in the IT world. Most of our integration architectures are API-driven and event-based. That is our focus. Coming back to your new technologies perspective, we want to reuse as much as possible and standardize versus going out and buying these one-off tools that solve for point-in-case use cases. We really don’t want to go down that path. For major processes, we do adopt a best-of-breed approach, but for, let’s say, site-based use cases where a specific site has a particular need for a tool, we try and standardize that and reuse what exists in a different site, for example. There may be some need for a business process change, minor process changes, but that is our direction to make those process changes and reuse what is there already in a different location or a different region. So, that’s one. Lastly, we are heavily aligned with SAP’s clean-core approach when it comes to customization. That has been the challenge for us over the last 25 years where we have been using SAP is our systems are heavily customized because we cater to different customers across the globe. Most of our demands are customer-driven, so we have to put in play these heavy customizations. But now we are taking a pause, and we are saying, “You know what? We have customized so much so far, but now we are moving our systems into RISE, which would enable a clean-core journey in the future.” Now we have to put really good governance criteria and review processes that do not allow heavy customization of our system. We want to move away from that model as much as possible. Again, it’s not easy to do that at this point in time, but there is always a start. Megan: I mean, it sounds like you took a very incremental, intentional approach to this. I mean, as you scaled globally then, what did modernization really look like at the company, and why start with integration? Harish: To that point, we have always looked at transformation, modernization, very objectively. For us, it’s just not about upgrading a system. That’s not what it is. Any modernization or transformation should add measurable business value is our model, is our charter. Having said that, we don’t look at modernization in terms of just upgrades, but in what it gets our business in terms of value. Most of our modernization transformation approaches are focused on connecting processes end-to-end across our supply chain, which is key for our business value. And then we also have a very concerted effort going on in the business community: how to standardize how our plants operate globally. Because, like I mentioned earlier, we have 100-plus plants, different processes, different legal regulations, different countries. It’s very hard for us to come up with one template across the globe, but we are trying to standardize as much as possible. And that’s where we are leveraging SAP’s Signavio, which is our business process management tool. We want to leverage Signavio’s capabilities in helping us standardize these global processes. Now, back to your question, why did integration come first? Because the backbone of any contemporary or modern organization is data. And to get the right data at the right time, integration is the key aspect of the whole optimization exercise. Data needed to flow seamlessly before we start optimizing or automating or even applying AI use cases. This is where integration came first. We wanted to create a single system of record across the operations. Well, when I say “single system of record,” it’s not just SAP, but the ability for us to create those data pipelines across those systems of record being supply chain, planning, inventory, et cetera, et cetera, in that operation space. The result is we want to get to a foundation that helps us scale consistently across our different region. That is our main objective is to, how do we scale as the business grows, as we develop into this bigger organization across different industries? How do we set this foundation that will help us scale consistently? Simplicity, consolidation becomes strategic assets at scale. Megan: Absolutely. And you touched on some of the complexities there of doing this at a scale that Jabil is at with its international footprint. What were some of the biggest challenges in your view in terms of rolling this out across regions, and how did that more standardized approach that you’ve mentioned there help? Harish: Absolutely. I would like to reiterate some of those key challenges I mentioned. One hundred-plus sites, different sites have different maturity levels in terms of how they approach processes. They have a multitude of different legacy systems, localized processes, workarounds, spreadsheets, and the change management that exists within each site is very different. And we do have a footprint of highly regulated businesses. And when it comes to regulated businesses, that comes with its own set of challenges around qualification and CSD processes, et cetera. These are the key challenges that we are up against. Now, the standardization helped us provide consistent workflows, data flows, and governance across sites. Now, we are not there at 100%, but we are working towards that, providing consistent workflows, data pipelines, and governance across sites. And we want to enable faster rollouts of our new bleeding edge technologies. For example, when I talked about SAP’s BTP or SAP Signavio or any other new SAP tool or non-SAP tool, traditionally our ability to deploy those had a challenge around the heavy customization that is required for each and every site. Now, the standardization approach takes that heavy customization out, which enables a faster rollout of those newer technologies. And then lastly, we want to scale across all of our plants. I think initially we want a target of about 40-plus plants with shared processes that are consistent across the different regions. We want to shift from a site-by-site operations model to more of an enterprise-capability approach. Megan: Right, and fascinating. And you touched on the people management aspect of this as well, because obviously this isn’t just about technology, it’s about people too. So, from the employee side, how did this shift to a more simplified landscape change the day-to-day experience for people compared to juggling multiple tools at once? Harish: Great question. And I’ve been hearing direct feedback from our business community on some of these transformation initiatives on how those have changed their daily jobs significantly. Before we embarked on this transformation journey, any employee, any persona. You take a buyer, you take an inventory planner, you take a finance analyst, we go by personas. They had to deal with multiple tools, manual coordination, data reconciliation, especially in the finance space, inconsistent processes across different regions. And then the time spent reconciling data resulted in delay of making decisions, robust decisions. This was the before. But now, since we are moving towards this newer standardization and more of an integration approach, we are able to achieve, to a certain extent, a single integrated workflow across different systems. We have built some key processes that will enable the single integrated workflows across systems. The users, our business community, irrespective of their roles in the organization, have clear visibility and shared data across their teams, which is very important. Earlier, they were dealing with different versions of the data, local workbooks, spreadsheets, and then the time spent talking to each other and reconciling what is the right data? What is the single source of truth? That we are trying to peel away that layer and get to that where the employees don’t have to deal with that kind of complexity. This reduces manual effort and enables faster issue resolution when it comes to actual disruptions. Employees move from chasing information to focusing on acting on insights, which is where I think the new age of AI comes into play. I’ll talk about that in a little bit, but technology becomes an enabler of decision-making, and it’s no more an overhead. That’s where we want to go. Megan: Fantastic. Such an important element of this, isn’t it, that people side of things? And we’ve touched briefly on this idea of value you’ve talked about before, because with an initiative of this scale, ROI is always front and center, of course. What benefits stood out most for you, and how important was better visibility in particular across systems? Harish: Megan, I talked about how modernization and transformation for Jabil means measurable business value, which is directly connected to the ROI. We don’t do any transformation initiatives just because we want to do it from an IT standpoint. Any investment that we make in a transformation or a modernization initiative has to have a deliverable business case that is approved, signed off by business, because that is the only way true transformation happens, if IT and business are a partner as part of this transformation journey. The biggest benefit that we have seen in this initiative is we are striving to reach, attain real-time visibility across our supply chain events. That is the biggest benefit that we see, faster response to disruptions and exceptions. And we are working to reduce our operational risk significantly by operating in this newer model. One example I can give you is the unified workflows that I talked about earlier. It enabled earlier identification of missing materials and faster resolution across our sites. When it comes to a manufacturing company that has a global footprint, materials are the backbone of our whole supply chain process, right? Having a unified workflow, which is able to identify missing materials early in the game, was a game changer for our whole operations community. Real-time analytics allow instant supply chain adjustments without delays. We are focusing a lot on getting analytics, a global analytic footprint in place that allows instant supply chain adjustments without any delays. That’s where AI is going to play a major role currently, and also in the near future. And again, when you talk about visibility. Visibility is not just about reporting what is there in the system. Visibility directly should enable scenario modeling for our users to make strategic adjustments in their processes, which visibility also should make way for proactive decision-making, and also foster business continuity. This is how we look at visibility at Jabil. Megan: Right. And you’re still on this journey, of course, but now that Jabil has a strong integration foundation in place, what does it unlock next for you, and how are you thinking about AI and automation as you’ve touched on a couple of times? Harish: Yeah, we have talked about a couple of times around AI. So, we strongly believe at Jabil, a strong integration foundation enables event-driven, real-time processes, robust decision-making, scalable automation, and all of this enable easier adoption of AI use cases. And again, we are in the new age of AI. We are working towards getting to a AI-enabled enterprise, but having these foundations in place truly fast tracks our approach of AI use cases. Our key focus areas, when I’m thinking about AI and automation in the immediate future, are predictive supply chain insights, intelligent exception handling, which is key to our business operations from a site operation standpoint. Intelligent exception handling is very, very key. On the supply chain side, I talked about predictive insights. That is also absolutely important. All of this enables AI-driven planning and forecasting capabilities. For us, AI should augment true decision-making and robust decision-making, and deliver measurable value, not just experiment AI in use cases. We want to move beyond just experimenting AI in our business processes, but we want that AI that we implement to truly augment the decision-making process that we have, and also deliver key business value. How does all this connect to integration? Integration ensures AI has access to trusted data, and also enables the ability to act across multiple systems in a global company like Jabil. Megan: Fantastic. And if we could just finish, I suppose, with a little bit of advice for others, for other leaders, perhaps, dealing with tool sprawl at the moment, what are some key lessons you would say you’ve learned about prioritizing integration right from the start? Harish: Absolutely. When it comes to tool sprawl, we can go all day about what are the different areas of tool sprawl? For example, application development, we have a multitude of tools; via integration, we have a multitude of tools. Data, we have a multitude of tools, but let’s just focus on integration. That’s the core topic here. I would recommend folks that are in transformative roles in their organizations to start with integration as a foundation and not as an afterthought, right? Prioritize simplification over adding a slew of different tools to address different capabilities. Try and simplify as much as possible before we start your upgrade or your transformation journey. Standardize over locally optimizing tools. Try and get to that. Try and get the business community, your key SMEs in the business space, to understand the value of standardization and simplification of processes and how that enables your business to deliver value faster. Second one, after prioritize: build a single source of truth for data as much as possible. I’m not saying it’s going to be always the case where an organization as in the scale of Jabil will be able to function just with SAP. They’re going to have different systems, but try and get to a model where you’re working with a single source of truth and not locally siloed data sources, right? Next is focus on building a scalable integration architecture. Don’t just confine yourselves to the current state where you are, and build something in place that will only serve you for the next six months to a year. No, that’s not the goal. Anything that you build as an integration architecture should be scalable, and should serve the organization for the next three to five years. That’s how I look at it. When I’m putting in a new architecture pattern or a new event-driven insights, I look at, “Okay, where is Jabil going to be two years, three years down the line? Would this suffice for that scale?” That’s how I look at it. Then focus on outcomes and not just technology. Focus on outcomes: speed, visibility, resilience, and not just technology deployment, because end of the day, IT and business should partner on the business value and not just technology upgrades. Going back, simplicity at scale is a very competitive advantage, and technology investments must tie directly to business value and operational resilience. That’s how we look at Jabil in terms of our tool sprawl and how we prioritize integration right from the start. And that’s what I would suggest to other leaders that are looking to advance in this space. Megan: Fantastic. Brilliant and very comprehensive advice. Thank you ever so much, Harish. And thank you ever so much for joining us. That was Harish Manohar, SAP IT Director at Jabil, whom I spoke with from Brighton in England. That’s it for this episode of Business Lab. I’m your host, Megan Tatum. I’m a contributing editor at Insights, the custom publishing division of MIT Technology Review. We were founded in 1899 at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, and you can find us in print, on the web, and at events each year around the world. For more information about us and the show, please check out our website at technologyreview.com. This show is available wherever you get your podcasts. And if you enjoyed this episode, we hope you’ll take a moment to rate and review us. Business Lab is a production of MIT Technology Review, and this episode was produced by Giro Studios. Thanks so much for listening. Goodbye. This content was produced by Insights, MIT Technology Review’s custom content arm, not its editorial staff. It was researched and written by humans, with any AI tools that may have been used limited to production processes under human oversight.
paragraphs: Simplifying and integrating enterprise technology can help companies move faster, respond to disruptions, and build a stronger foundation for AI, says Harish Manohar, SAP IT Director at Jabil.

As companies scale, the technology supporting operations can become a liability just as quickly as it becomes an asset. Disconnected systems, site-specific tools, spreadsheets, and manual workarounds can create data silos that make it harder to spot problems early, coordinate responses, and make decisions with confidence. For Jabil, a global manufacturing company with more than 100 sites across more than 30 countries, the answer has been to make integration and simplification a priority.

That philosophy also changes how Jabil approaches modernization. “Any modernization or transformation should add measurable business value,” Manohar says. The company is focused on connecting processes end-to-end across its supply chain and creating a foundation that can scale consistently across regions. Integration comes first because, as Manohar puts it, “the backbone of any contemporary or modern organization is data.” Before organizations can optimize, automate, or apply AI, data needs to flow seamlessly across systems.

But doing that across a global organization is hardly straightforward. Jabil’s more than 100 sites operate with different levels of process maturity, legacy systems, and localized workflows, while regulated businesses bring additional compliance requirements. As such, standardizing across different regions and business environments means changing processes and governance without disrupting the operations already in place.

The value of that work extends beyond the technology to the people using it. Integrated workflows can offer employees shared visibility into data, reduce manual data reconciliation, and help them move from chasing information to acting on insights. For Jabil, the aim is also to improve real-time visibility into supply chain events, which can enable faster responses to disruptions and reduce operational risk.

draft_context.source_title: With Gemini 3.8 Flash, Google reminds everyone it's still in the race
draft_context.description: Google on Wednesday announced the release of Gemini 3.8 Flash in an attempt to reclaim its reputation as a top-tier model maker in the process. The company's commitment to the frontier model race has been in doubt since at least early August when Google DeepMind CEO Demis Hassabis stepped down to become chairman of the AI research biz and Koray Kavukcuoglu took over leadership under a less exalted title, SVP. Google CEO Sundar Pichai's reassurances weren't particularly convincing in light of the company's failure to release Gemini 3.5 Pro in June as promised. Nor were they helped by the modest benchmark metrics of Gemini 3.5 Flash, which, while speedy and cost-efficient, have been overshadowed in terms of intelligence scores by open-weight models from Chinese AI companies over the past few months. But Google has been iterating rapidly. Gemini 3.8 Flash is its fourth Flash model in as many months and it has improved enough to be considered alongside the highest scoring models in terms of intelligence while also being performant and relatively affordable – at least until its introductory price ($0.75/M input tokens, $3.75/M output tokens) doubles in the new year. "Gemini 3.8 Flash delivers substantial gains from 3.7 Flash, often approaching the performance of higher-cost frontier models," said Tulsee Doshi, Google senior director of product management, and Raluca Ada Popa, Gemini Security Lead at Google DeepMind, in a blog post. "On DeepSWE v1.1 (Long-Horizon Software Engineering) 3.8 Flash outperforms most larger frontier models in autonomously solving complex engineering problems end to end, only at a fraction of the cost." Gemini 3.8 Flash, set to high reasoning, scores 59 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, an increase of three points from its predecessor. That puts it level with GPT-5.6 Sol (extra high, 59) and Grok 4.6 (medium, 59). From there, current intelligence rankings, based on nine benchmarks, are: GLM-5.3 (max, 60), Kimi K3 (max, 60), Grok 4.6 (high, 61), GPT-5.6 Sol (max, 61), Claude Opus 5 (max, 63), and Claude Fable 5.1 (max, 66). At $0.58 per Intelligence Index task, Gemini 3.8 Flash is "the cheapest model at its level of intelligence," according to Artificial Analysis. As a point of comparison, Anthropic's latest general usage flagship model, Fable 5.1, costs about 6x more – $3.76 per Intelligence Index task. Gemini 3.8 Flash costs about 40 percent more per task than its similarly priced predecessor because it tends to output more tokens and to execute more turns when acting as an agent. "3.8 Flash works harder," explain Doshi and Popa. "On complex tasks, it exhibits greater diligence – executing extra reasoning steps, and calling tools iteratively. At times, the model might use more tokens to maximize performance, especially at higher effort levels." The two Googlers also note that Gemini 3.8 Flash shows improvements in benchmarks relevant to enterprise knowledge work, like Vals Finance Agent V2, Harvey's Legal Agent Benchmark, and HLE-Verified. Gemini 3.8 Flash is available for developers through Google Antigravity, the Gemini API in Google AI Studio and Android Studio, and interface design service Stitch. Enterprises can use Gemini Enterprise. Consumers with Google AI Pro and Ultra subscriptions can access the model via the Gemini app, AI Mode in Google Search, and Gemini in Google Sheets. Google has also launched the Fairwind Program to provide governments, critical infrastructure organizations, and software maintainers with access to Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber, a version of the model tuned for software vulnerability hunting and remediation. ®

article.title: Google ra Gemini 3.8 Flash, vẫn chưa thấy bản Pro đâu
article.summary: Ngày 2/9, Google ra mắt Gemini 3.8 Flash và biến thể an ninh mạng Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber, chỉ một ngày sau khi Anthropic tung Claude Fable 5.1 và Mythos 5.1. Nhưng trong khi Anthropic nâng cấp thẳng vào dòng model mạnh nhất của mình, Google lại tiếp tục đưa ra một bản Flash, phân khúc tầm trung giá rẻ, thay vì Gemini 3.5 Pro, model đầu bảng mà giới công nghệ chờ đợi suốt nhiều tháng qua.

sections.body: Đây đã là bản Flash thứ ba Google ra mắt chỉ trong 6 tuần, sau Gemini 3.6 Flash ngày 21/7 và Gemini 3.7 Flash ngày 13/8. Trong khi đó, Gemini 3.5 Pro, model đầu bảng thực sự của hãng, vẫn chưa có ngày ra mắt cụ thể, dù CEO Sundar Pichai từng nói hồi tháng 7 rằng model đang được thử nghiệm cùng đối tác. Đầu tháng 8, Google cũng thay nhân sự cấp cao tại DeepMind: Demis Hassabis rời vị trí điều hành hàng ngày để giữ vai trò Chủ tịch, còn Koray Kavukcuoglu, cựu Giám đốc công nghệ DeepMind, tiếp quản việc phát triển Gemini và báo cáo trực tiếp cho Sundar Pichai.

sections.heading: Ai nên chú ý lúc này
sections.body: Về giá, Gemini 3.8 Flash giữ nguyên mức giới thiệu của bản 3.7 Flash: 0,75 USD cho mỗi triệu token đầu vào và 3,75 USD cho mỗi triệu token đầu ra, tương đương khoảng 19.700 đồng và 98.600 đồng, áp dụng đến hết năm 2026. Từ 1/1/2027, giá tăng lên 1,50 USD và 7,50 USD, tương đương khoảng 39.400 đồng và 197.000 đồng.

sections.heading: Điều cần theo dõi tiếp
sections.body: Google cho biết Gemini 3.8 Flash vượt phần lớn model đầu bảng lớn hơn trên DeepSWE v1.1, benchmark đo khả năng tự giải quyết các bài toán kỹ thuật phần mềm dài hơi, dù chi phí thấp hơn nhiều. Model cũng dẫn trước cả Gemini 3.7 Flash lẫn các model đầu bảng khác trên hai benchmark chuyên ngành Vals Finance Agent V2 và Harvey Legal Agent Benchmark, đồng thời đạt 54,9% trên HLE-Verified, bài kiểm tra suy luận nhiều bước trải rộng các lĩnh vực khoa học, nhân văn và chuyên môn. Cách model đạt điểm cao là "làm việc chăm hơn": tự thêm bước suy luận, gọi công cụ nhiều lần hơn, có thể tốn nhiều token hơn khi đặt mức effort cao. Google khuyên hạ effort nếu ưu tiên tiết kiệm chi phí, hoặc tiếp tục dùng Gemini 3.7 Flash cho các tác vụ cần hiệu quả token.

draft_context.description: Bản cập nhật Flash thứ ba trong 6 tuần của Google xuất hiện đúng lúc Anthropic vừa nâng cấp toàn bộ dòng model hàng đầu.
paragraphs: Ngày 2/9, Google ra mắt Gemini 3.8 Flash và biến thể an ninh mạng Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber, chỉ một ngày sau khi Anthropic tung Claude Fable 5.1 và Mythos 5.1. Nhưng trong khi Anthropic nâng cấp thẳng vào dòng model mạnh nhất của mình, Google lại tiếp tục đưa ra một bản Flash, phân khúc tầm trung giá rẻ, thay vì Gemini 3.5 Pro, model đầu bảng mà giới công nghệ chờ đợi suốt nhiều tháng qua.
Google công bố Gemini 3.8 Flash và 3.8 Flash Cyber trên blog chính thức

Đây đã là bản Flash thứ ba Google ra mắt chỉ trong 6 tuần, sau Gemini 3.6 Flash ngày 21/7 và Gemini 3.7 Flash ngày 13/8. Trong khi đó, Gemini 3.5 Pro, model đầu bảng thực sự của hãng, vẫn chưa có ngày ra mắt cụ thể, dù CEO Sundar Pichai từng nói hồi tháng 7 rằng model đang được thử nghiệm cùng đối tác. Đầu tháng 8, Google cũng thay nhân sự cấp cao tại DeepMind: Demis Hassabis rời vị trí điều hành hàng ngày để giữ vai trò Chủ tịch, còn Koray Kavukcuoglu, cựu Giám đốc công nghệ DeepMind, tiếp quản việc phát triển Gemini và báo cáo trực tiếp cho Sundar Pichai.

Google cho biết Gemini 3.8 Flash vượt phần lớn model đầu bảng lớn hơn trên DeepSWE v1.1, benchmark đo khả năng tự giải quyết các bài toán kỹ thuật phần mềm dài hơi, dù chi phí thấp hơn nhiều. Model cũng dẫn trước cả Gemini 3.7 Flash lẫn các model đầu bảng khác trên hai benchmark chuyên ngành Vals Finance Agent V2 và Harvey Legal Agent Benchmark, đồng thời đạt 54,9% trên HLE-Verified, bài kiểm tra suy luận nhiều bước trải rộng các lĩnh vực khoa học, nhân văn và chuyên môn. Cách model đạt điểm cao là "làm việc chăm hơn": tự thêm bước suy luận, gọi công cụ nhiều lần hơn, có thể tốn nhiều token hơn khi đặt mức effort cao. Google khuyên hạ effort nếu ưu tiên tiết kiệm chi phí, hoặc tiếp tục dùng Gemini 3.7 Flash cho các tác vụ cần hiệu quả token.

sections.heading: Các nguồn đang khớp nhau ở đâu
sections.body: Điểm đáng chú ý nhất nằm ở giá. Gemini 3.8 Flash được cung cấp với mức 0,75 USD/1 triệu token đầu vào và 3,75 USD/1 triệu token đầu ra, đúng bằng mức giá giới thiệu của Gemini 3.7 Flash. Với các nhà phát triển sử dụng API ở quy mô lớn, chi phí thấp có thể trở thành lợi thế đáng kể khi triển khai những tác vụ AI cần xử lý liên tục.

sections.heading: Tác động thực tế với người đọc
sections.body: Nhưng Google không đơn thuần tung ra một model giá rẻ. Gemini 3.8 Flash được thiết kế cho những công việc đòi hỏi nhiều bước suy luận, viết phần mềm trong thời gian dài và vận hành các AI agent có khả năng tự thực hiện nhiệm vụ. Trên benchmark DeepSWE v1.1 dành cho kỹ thuật phần mềm dài hạn, Google cho biết Gemini 3.8 Flash có thể tự giải quyết các vấn đề kỹ thuật phức tạp từ đầu đến cuối và vượt qua phần lớn những frontier model lớn hơn, với chi phí chỉ bằng một phần.

sections.heading: Ai nên chú ý lúc này
sections.body: Cách Gemini 3.8 Flash xử lý các nhiệm vụ phức tạp cũng khác đáng kể so với một chatbot chỉ cố gắng đưa ra câu trả lời nhanh. Google cho biết model có xu hướng thực hiện thêm các bước suy luận, gọi công cụ nhiều lần và sử dụng thêm token khi cần thiết để nâng chất lượng kết quả. Người dùng cũng có thể giảm mức độ suy luận để tiết kiệm token trong những trường hợp ưu tiên hiệu quả chi phí.

sections.heading: Điều cần theo dõi tiếp
sections.body: Chính ở đây, cái tên “Flash” trở nên đáng chú ý. Tốc độ không chỉ là một tuyên bố marketing của Google. Trong một thử nghiệm được chia sẻ trong cộng đồng, cùng một prompt được sử dụng để so sánh Gemini 3.8 Flash với Opus 5 cho một tác vụ build, Gemini hoàn thành trong 37 giây, trong khi Opus 5 mất 24 phút. Đây là thử nghiệm của người dùng chứ không phải benchmark chính thức của Google, nhưng kết quả cho thấy tốc độ của Gemini 3.8 Flash đang là một trong những điểm gây ấn tượng mạnh nhất.

draft_context.source_title: Apple iPhone Ultra vs. Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8: It could just come down to one thing
draft_context.description: Apple iPhone Ultra A bold new entrant The iPhone Ultra is set to usher in the age of the foldable iPhone, and leaks point to a device that has the potential to be truly noteworthy. Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Short and sweet The Z Fold 8 is uniquely interesting, and while it may not have the best cameras, it makes foldable fun to use. Apple iPhone Ultra vs. Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8: Pricing and availability (Image credit: Derrek Lee / Android Central) The iPhone Ultra is slated to make its debut at Apple's launch event on September 9, 2026. The foldable could cost anywhere between $2,000 to $2,500, and we'll have to wait until the event to know the official pricing. But with Apple hiking prices on most of its products in the last two months, it's a given that this year's iPhones will see price increases across the board. Even if the iPhone Ultra is unveiled alongside the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, it may not actually show up at the same time — the latest leaks point to general availability later in the year. Again, that's something we will know definitely on September 9. Given the cost, it is projected that the foldable will be available in limited quantities — much like the Galaxy Z TriFold — and it remains to be seen if it will be sold in all regions simultaneously. Samsung unveiled the Galaxy Z Fold 8 on July 22, 2026, and the foldable retails at $1,899. This is the base model with 256GB of storage, and there's also a 512GB edition that costs $2,099 in the U.S., and a 1TB model that is $2,499. Apple iPhone Ultra vs. Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8: Design (Image credit: Nicholas Sutrich / Android Central) The iPhone Ultra will be different to every other iPhone thus far, with the foldable design ushering in an entirely new form factor for iOS. Leaks point to the iPhone Ultra having a similar wide-and-short configuration as the Galaxy Z Fold 8, and the passport-style design is definitely intriguing — there's no wonder that other Android manufacturers are emulating a similar style. Leaks point to a 5.5-inch cover panel and a 7.8-inch inner panel, and the iPhone Ultra could be as thin as 4.5mm while unfolded, bringing it in line with the Z Fold 8 and other Android foldables. The design looks a lot like the Pixel 11 Pro Fold , with rounded edges and a flatter profile along the hinge. While Apple introduced a bright orange color with the iPhone 17 Pro , the iPhone Ultra is said to be available in muted colors, including white and black. Just like Android foldables, the iPhone Ultra may see Touch ID housed within the power button as the standard mode of authentication instead of Face ID. The Z Fold 8 gets a 5.5-inch cover panel and a 7.6-inch inner screen, and Samsung managed to deliver IP48 dust and water resistance. Interestingly, one of the biggest selling points of the iPhone Ultra could be a display without anu visible crease. The Find N6 and Vivo X Fold 5 do a fabulous job in this regard — they're better than the Galaxy Z Fold 8 and Fold 8 Ultra — and with the iPhone Ultra touted to use two layers of ultra-thin glass and a liquid-metal hinge, it is entirely possible that Apple's foldable will debut with a creaseless design, outshining Samsung's Z Fold 8 in this key area. Apple iPhone Ultra vs. Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8: Hardware (Image credit: Apple / Android Central) The iPhone Ultra will see the biggest battery of any iPhone, and that in itself is exciting. Leaks point to a 4,883mAh battery, and that's similar to what's available on the Z Fold 8. That said, iOS has much better efficiency in general, so the iPhone Ultra should have better battery life, and with Apple touted to switch to a 2nm node, battery life could get an additional boost. Category Apple iPhone Ultra (based on leaks) Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Display Outer: 5.5-inch ProMotion LTPO OLED, 2088 x 1422 Inner: 7.8-inch ProMotion LTPO OLED Outer: 5.5-inch 120Hz LTPO AMOLED, 1972 x 1248 Inner: 7.6-inch 120Hz LTPO AMOLED, 2448 x 1848 Operating System iOS 27, at least seven updates One UI 9 (Android 17), seven updates Chipset Apple A20, 2nm Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 for Galaxy, 3nm RAM 12GB 12GB/16GB Storage 256GB, 512GB, 1TB, 2TB 256GB, 512GB, 1TB Rear cameras Main: 48MP f/1.8, sensor-shift OIS Wide-angle: 48MP f/2.2 Main: 50MP f/1.8, OIS Wide-angle: 50MP f/1.9 Front camera 24MP 10MP (internal), 10MP (external) Battery 4,883mAh 4,800mAh (dual 2,400mAh cells) Charging 40W iPhone 17 Pro, 25W MagSafe/Qi 2 45W wired, 20W wireless Dimensions Folded: 120.6 x 83.8 x 9.2mm Unfolded: 120.6 x 167.6 x 4.5mm Folded: 123.9 x 81.9 x 9.7mm Unfolded: 123.9 x 161.4 x 4.5mm Wide foldables are smaller than book-style devices like the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra , and as a result, Samsung just went with two cameras on the Galaxy Z Fold 8: a 50MP main camera and 50MP wide-angle lens. The iPhone Ultra is likely to use a similar arrangement, and leaks point to two 48MP cameras, without a dedicated tele lens. We'll need to wait and see if that pans out, but as someone who uses the telephoto lens constantly, I would like to see this on the foldable. Apple iPhone Ultra vs. Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8: Software (Image credit: Derrek Lee / Android Central) Software makes a big difference on a foldable, with the added real estate ideal to multitask. This is a priority in iOS 27, and there's no doubt that the iPhone Ultra will get a lot of the same features that we've seen on Android foldables over the last two years, including a task bar, floating windows, and multitasking features. Samsung does a good job in this area with the Galaxy Z Fold 8, and I'm interested in seeing how the iPhone Ultra will hold up against Samsung's foldable. Apple iPhone Ultra vs. Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8: Which should you buy? (Image credit: AppleTrack) While foldables have been around for the better part of a decade now, they're still pretty niche. That will change with the introduction of the iPhone Ultra; say what you will about Apple, but the brand has an unmatched ability to grab attention, and interest in foldables will skyrocket following the iPhone Ultra launch. Now, whether this will translate to sales is another thing entirely, but if you're an iPhone user and wanted to switch to a foldable, you don't need to wait long to get one running iOS. While Samsung got a lot right with the Z Fold 8, it doesn't do nearly enough to convince iOS users to move to Android in any meaningful numbers. Apple iPhone Ultra A bold new entrant The iPhone Ultra is set to launch soon, and with a similar design as the Z Fold 8 but with iOS, it could just be the device that convinces iPhone users to switch to a foldable. Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Short and sweet Samsung nailed the brief with the Galaxy Z Fold 8, and the unique size of the foldable makes it stand out. ]]>

article.title: Anker’s Eufy Strides Into IFA With a New AI Ecosystem and Devices to Match

I’m no stranger to AI in home security , but Eufy’s approach is unique and has the potential to be particularly advantageous for customers.

draft_context.source_title: Anker’s Eufy Strides Into IFA With a New AI Ecosystem and Devices to Match
draft_context.description: Anker's security division has big plans, and the company is prepping an even bigger AI management system for your home -- without relying on cloud data or subscriptions.
paragraphs: Anker and its home brand Eufy came to Berlin’s IFA event well prepared with major news, including an overhaul of how the company approaches home security, and the new capabilities it wants to give devices in the coming years. I’m no stranger to AI in home security , but Eufy’s approach is unique and has the potential to be particularly advantageous for customers.

Anker’s flagship announcement is an excellent example of what I’m talking about. We saw the company’s newest MindBase hub, a home AI enabler made to connect to many kinds of other Anker and Eufy products and process their data with AI algorithms, all entirely on-device. That means no connections to the cloud, few worries about how the company will use your private data for analysis and lower costs than most AI around the home .

Using Anker’s EasyOmni Link platform, the MindBase is supposed to connect to Anker’s security, energy , cleaning and audio devices. It also has Matter support, so devices that work with Apple Home, Amazon Alexa and Google Home are also on the table. The base uses an in-house-developed LLM running on an AI chip to accomplish much of what most companies need cloud help to do.
While Anker didn’t show off everything the MindBase is capable of, we did get some more advanced looks of its security capabilities thanks to Eufy’s new security line, set for the months to come.

Eufy is also releasing a new wired video doorbell , notable for its 3K resolution and AI tracking technolog y (meaning it can keep delivery people in view for longer, etc.). It’s set for sale at $300 later this month.

For those who want a full security setup, Eufy is also launching an eight-channel NVR system with 2K security cameras. I’m not sure how many NVR features will need MindBase to function, but Anker says the wired, fully contained kit can handle auto framing, smart video searches, cross-camera tracking and 24/7 recording.

draft_context.source_title: How Sonos rebooted itself
draft_context.description: Today, I’m talking with Tom Conrad, the CEO of Sonos. Tom and I have known each other for a long time — he was the chief technology officer of Pandora, VP of product at Snap, and the chief product officer of Quibi. He was also on the board at Sonos during its disastrous 2024 app redesign that threatened to crash the entire brand. Tom took over as interim CEO to right the ship during that period, and then took the permanent role just about a year ago. As you’ll hear him say, he thinks Sonos is fully out of that period now, and on to its next chapter with a huge product and platform launch called Sonos 27 . Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here . Not a subscriber? You can sign up here . I mean, come on, you all listen to the show. That is all the most Decoder bait imaginable. I have been dying to have Tom on the show to talk about how the board decided to move on from previous CEO Patrick Spence, how he diagnosed the issues inside the company, and what decisions he made to fix them. Those fixes involved a lot of big changes: to the company’s structure, its product lineup, and how it thinks about itself and what its product fundamentally is. That’s that new platform, Sonos 27, which you’ll hear Tom call a new foundation for the company that makes every Sonos product work better as part of a system. There’s a lot here, including how AI assistants can work across the system, the idea of having a mesh network of little computers in your home disguised as speakers, and of course, the testy relationship between Sonos and Google, which means Google’s Gemini assistant isn’t available on Sonos devices. Oh, and of course we got into the weeds about smart home standards, because I am a smart home nerd and simply cannot help myself. But to his credit, Tom was willing to nerd out with me, and I think this conversation is pretty fun because of it. Okay: Sonos CEO Tom Conrad. Here we go. This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity. Tom Conrad, you’re the CEO of Sonos. Welcome to Decoder . Thank you. As they say, it’s so great to be here. I am just going to say, finally, I have been asking you to be on the show for at least a year, if not before. I think the first time I met you was in the back of a car at CES when you were at Pandora. Sounds right. One hundred years ago. One hundred years ago. We were children. [Laughs] We were little babies. That car was driven by a human driver. That’s how far back it was. That’s right. And then you took a turn through Quibi. You and I talked through that, and now you’re at Sonos. As you know, I’m a huge fan of Sonos. We had your predecessor, Patrick Spence, on the show a bunch of times . Many things have happened, so I just want to start at the very beginning of this. You’re about a year into being the permanent CEO of Sonos. You have a bunch of news to announce. Just tell us what you think Sonos is today. What is your conception of this company? When I came in the door, one of my earliest observations was that the company behaved like it was 100 percent hardware, but we’re really 100 percent hardware and 100 percent software. And if you get either one of those even a little bit wrong, the impact is tremendous. So how does that show up really day-to-day? It was about returning the company to the idea that Sonos doesn’t make these individual products, but we really make one thing — we make the Sonos system. It all has to hang together in a cohesive, interesting, and valuable way, or we’re just not doing the work. There’s been a bunch of basic blocking and tackling, of course, both operationally and in the work that we’re doing in the product family. But at the highest level, returning the company to the idea that we are a system for audio in the home has been the highest-level mantra. When you say come into the company, do you mean as a board member or as the CEO? I mean, let’s start the starter pistol in January of 2025, 18 months ago, when I stepped in first as interim CEO and then was lucky enough six months later to be asked to take the job more permanently. The reason I asked that question is that you obviously have two different views of the company in different roles. We did have former CEO Patrick Spence on several occasions, and he said something very similar to me when he first took over — that Sonos was stuck in its ways. It was really focused on very, very slow iterations of hardware. He tried very hard to push the metabolism of the company to be much faster, and he talked about that very openly with me. That led eventually to what I think is a moment of true crisis: the app launch. It was a disaster. The system stopped working. That’s when you came in to right the ship. Tell me about that gap. You came in, and you said this company thinks it’s a hardware company. That’s what your predecessor had been saying, but it went sideways in big, meaningful ways. Tell me about that moment and why you think it was the same conception even when you came in. So as you describe, I’ve been involved with the company going back almost 20 years. We brought Pandora to Sonos in 2007, I think, and I was able to get to know the company as a partner before I got to know it as a board member. I came onto the board in 2016 right as Patrick became CEO. So from the vantage point of a board member, I got to participate in Patrick’s chapter. I guess the way I would characterize his high-order thinking about the company in those early days was that, as you described, he wanted to turn the company into a product execution machine with an emphasis on hardware products. We call them NPIs, or new product introductions. In the chapter before him, it was sometimes years between new Sonos products. Spence said, “Look, we’re going to make a company that knows how to ship a couple of great new products a year.” And he did that. I mean, the company has reliably shipped a couple of great products, hardware products, every year, for close to a decade now. Sometimes, when you energize an organization around an idea, there are unintended consequences. I think one unintended consequence of that framing was that the company became very focused on the individual products, one at a time. Even as a board member, I received Roam as a portable speaker with a certain amount of battery life, waterproofing, and Bluetooth connectivity. I didn’t really think about it as a member of the Sonos system. Even with the software work that we did, and with every product that we make, there is a tremendous amount of software effort and innovation that goes into them. But even the software that we made was very focused on the individual NPIs. “What can we do in software to differentiate Move 2 from other speakers in that category?” What was hard to do, and what was hard to prioritize in the company, was horizontal slices of software experiences that benefited all of the platform. So, in a way, I think some of that debt accumulated, and the company thought that the antidote was to recreate the app experience. And as you know, we made a bunch of mistakes at that moment. I’m really proud of the fact that I think we’re well beyond that chapter now, but we could have been much more thoughtful about how we qualified that product in the real world. We could have been much more thoughtful about how we rolled it out to customers. We could have, candidly, I think, examined the original impetus in the first place. It was very Sonos-motivated. We wanted to put the app on a modern architecture to make us more nimble. In my chapter at Sonos, I’m really trying to bring it all back to how we can focus on the customer first. I’m so inspired by talking to people on social media and in my inbox, and people in the industry, like you, about how we show up and solve the real problems that are happening in real households. I’m so excited about the things we’re going to talk to you about today because I think they’re really an answer to many of those questions. If you’re a listener, you know I’m familiar with Tom. The man’s on Threads doing customer support every day. And actually, I should not take advantage of this. I hold myself back from asking you for direct customer support all the time. Anytime. The way that you can tell it’s actually me and not our crackerjack social team is that I often will let a Thread die before I should or fail to follow up with someone. So if we were executing perfectly on that, you would know it was fake Tom, but it’s real Tom, and I do it when I can, but sometimes imperfectly. At least it’s not an AI avatar Tom. That’s when we know it’s going to go sideways. [Laughs] That’s right. I know you’re a Decoder fan, so I’m going to make you sit in this for just one more moment because I find all of this to be really fascinating. The app shipped, and the feedback was immediately and intensely negative. Many, many things were broken. Speakers weren’t working at weddings. This is a time of massive crisis. The company goes to resolve it, but then you’re on the board, and it’s clear that there’s going to be a leadership transition, that Patrick needs to go, and we need a new CEO. You’re going to be the interim CEO. Tell us about that process. Very, very few people will ever be in that kind of process or get insight into that process. What happened? What were the steps? Well, I guess you start by saying that the last thing as a board that you want to do is to remove a CEO, particularly one who had as many successes as Patrick had. But I think as we looked at the company’s progress recovering from the app crisis, and frankly the tenor of the conversation inside the company, we just decided that for this kind of step-function improvement we needed on some of these dimensions, we had to make some changes in leadership, and that included a CEO change. It was a wild experience for me because, I’ll tell you, at no point in the decade leading up to that day in January did I imagine that I might end up the CEO of Sonos. But in the process, the board asked if I’d be willing to step in on an interim basis, and it was an easy yes for me. It’s a cliché, but I’m a customer, and I love this product. There was a Sonos Move in the room when my daughter was born. You talked about weddings. I was watching friends and colleagues on the internet, frustrated by their experience. I wanted to come in and fix it. Of course, as a board member, I felt some real culpability in it. So [I was] thrilled at the chance to come in. When you’re an interim CEO, the assignment is really to keep the wheels on. The assignment at Sonos specifically was to right the ship. So during the period when the board was doing their comprehensive search for the person that they would ultimately decide was the right choice for the company, it was really easy for me to show up and just do that hard work of trying to get the company back on track. While I never imagined that I would land in this seat, I feel so blessed that it happened. I do love this job and continue to love the company and the team, and I’m so excited about the things we’re doing for our customers. Very few people are going to get an interview to become the CEO of Sonos. I imagine at some point you went from being the interim CEO to wanting to become the permanent CEO. What was that process like? Did you write a memo? Was there a pitch deck? What were the steps? Yeah, so there were a couple of pitch moments that the board asked me, completely reasonably, to engage in the process of applying for the job in the same way that all of the other talented candidates that they spoke to engaged. And so I took a personality test. Wait, you did? Yeah. With the letters? Oh, yeah. Like an ENTJ or whatever? Oh, yeah. One of the letter things, sure. They wanted to know what they were getting. Do they know that that is basically just like astrology? Someone should tell them. You know what? Yep, yep. I presented my vision for the company more than once, and I had the incredible advantage of being inside the four walls of the company and deeply understanding what was working and what wasn’t, and the things that we needed to do to get to this next chapter. It was a period of intense, intense work for me and everybody around me at the company, and more than a little anxiety about how it was going to turn out. It was so fun, though, to get the call and then to just immediately be able to pivot at least a fraction of the work from the entirely tactical to the much more strategic, to begin to talk about what kind of company we are going to build together in this next chapter. When it was announced that you would become the permanent CEO, even when you were the interim CEO, my reaction was, “Oh, this makes sense.” To use a football analogy, football teams hire defensive head coaches and offensive head coaches, and they come from one side of the ball or the other. It was just obvious: “Oh, this company needs a software CEO, and Tom is a software guy.” You’re describing a situation where obviously it’s both. You’ve got hardware and software together, but that was the light that went off in my head — “Oh, this is a software person coming in to fix a big software problem.” Is that how you saw it initially? Yeah, my career started with selling personal computers in 1986 or something, at the original Micro Center. If you’ve ever been to a Micro Center, it’s one of the few remaining big-box retailers for computers. So at the original Micro Center in Columbus, Ohio, at 16 years old, I walked into the CEO’s office and said, “I want to work here.” So from my earliest days, I was sitting with early adopters of personal computers and watching their struggles to understand the technology and put it to use in their lives. I became an engineer and a product designer out of a desire to help people learn to use these products. And that’s really what’s motivated me through my entire career: how do I help teams make great experiences? So while it’s true that I’m a software person, 35 years in the business, my identity really is as a product designer. And I’d like to think that the board imagined that, yes, they needed a software person, but they needed somebody who could holistically look at the opportunity across hardware and software and help the team get there. You appear to be through it now. There’s a big stack of announcements here, including MCP integration. I’ve got a lot of questions about all that. When you became the permanent CEO 18 months ago, you said you immediately shifted strategy. What brought that into focus for you? “Oh, this is actually a software platform with hardware components”? Was that instinct? Was it research? Was it, “I’m getting through this app process, and that is becoming revealed to me”? How did that work? I think by disposition I’m a fairly right-brained person, and I have this intuitive feeling — creative, or whatever the words are, not as quantitative. But my first job out of college was at Apple, and I think even from the early days when I was there, we talked about the intersection of the arts and humanities and the sciences. I think one lesson of my career has been that you really do have an obligation to bring both a quant and a qual assessment to most things that pass your desk. So the development of our strategy was very much like that. Yes, there was an intuitive sense about what the right answer for Sonos was that was built up from my experience as a customer by observing our customers and talking to them through the years. A piece of that is a perspective about where the puck is going, of course. But I do have access to piles and piles and piles of data about how our products behave in the real world, how our customers interact with them, what they use, what they don’t use, and lots of people around me in the organization who can bring that quantitative framing. I think one advantage I had over other CEO candidates was that I could bring some of that horsepower to bear on the story that I shared with the board about my vision for the future of the company. You’ve made some changes. It’s time for the Decoder questions. You have restructured the company. There have been a few rounds of layoffs. How big is Sonos today? We’re about 1,500 people. And how is that structured? So the company that I stepped into was divided into business units. We had a team that was focused on home. We had a team that was focused on the professional opportunity, a team that was focused on home theater, and so on. While there’s something to be said for P&L responsibilities, et cetera, et cetera, et cetera, there’s something to be said for that approach at a certain scale. I think that my appraisal was that we were sub-scale for the inefficiencies that creep in. We have the almost guaranteed duplication of effort across the silos. What’s more, if you imagine that the product is really the system, the idea that your portables team sits far away from your home theater team, and sits far away from your plugged-in speakers team, is almost surely going to run counter to the kind of progress that you’re trying to motivate. And so very quickly, within three weeks of my arrival, we reorganized the company into a functional model. So my leadership team today, of course, has a finance organization, a legal organization, a sales organization, and a marketing organization. But the product team now shows up as represented by hardware, software, and global supply chain operations, so leaders across each of those things. And what that allows us to do is to assemble cross-functional teams, or matrix-style teams, to invest in the initiatives that are of the highest priority to our customers and to the business at any given moment. And we can flex that up and down and side to side as our needs change. We might, for an interval, be very focused on this part of the portfolio over here, and then we might be able to move to focusing on a different corner of the portfolio. No one has to get a new boss, and people can fluidly move from these things and get new opportunities to learn. It just strikes me as a much more appropriate organizational structure for our current stage. You’re describing the shift from a divisional structure to a vastly more functional structure. Yes. That’s Apple, right? Yep, sure. Everyone comes up, and there’s one big product meeting. You obviously make a lot of software. I’ve described you as a software CEO. It seems like the software industry is in a moment of existential crisis about how software is made, about what a product manager versus an engineer versus a designer do. Are you still in the classic structures of building software? Or has AI completely upended what you’re doing? No, we’re as deep in this as anyone. What’s been really fun for me over the course of the last year is to watch the software engineering team go from thoughtful skepticism to pretty deep embrace, if I’m honest. Some of that is on the back of just how dramatically the tools have evolved over the course of the last 12 months, certainly. I think almost everyone in the industry went home at the holidays at the tail end of 2025, coming into 2026, and came back just gobsmacked by how much progress the frontier labs were making on agentic coding, and it’s been a real accelerant for us. As complex as this transition is, I’m really excited about being able to help our engineers navigate what’s a pretty fundamental sea change in the way that this kind of infrastructure gets built, and it’s fun to get to be a part of that at this moment. Did you break up the classic PM, designer, and engineer triad? Or is that still the core building block? We still have all three, but it blurs particularly as the designers and the product managers can be prototypers at a really high level with incredible efficiency. It’s exciting to see how quickly they can communicate their ideas now in a medium that just didn’t exist at all for them a year ago. We’re at the turn, right? You came in, you restructured the company, you identified a new thesis for the company. Today you’re here to talk about all the new news. Do you think you’re through it? Do you think the existing customers have forgiven you for the app mess? Do you think the brand has been restored? Yeah, as we’ve been saying, I think that there’s the quant and there’s the qual. The quant is green across the board. Performance, reliability, customer care interactions, social tone, NPS — these things are all restored to levels that we enjoyed before any of that happened. On the qualitative side, I love the fact that I can show up on Reddit or on social media broadly and engage with our customers and have a constructive conversation about things that they’re excited that we’re doing, and things where we’re still disappointing an individual customer on some dimension.
