This is not anything to do with big AI integrations or the new MCP way to address the Sonos system. Those are big ideas, and I’m just insistently dragging you back down into the dirt of: if the internet goes out, are the lights still going to turn on? You don’t want to be the partner that puts in the internet-connected light switches that don’t work when the internet is down. But it’s not just the internet-connected light switches; it’s the logic of making it all work together. I understand. Yeah, fair. Here’s what I’ll say about that. For 40 years now, we’ve been talking about technology for the home, starting with the personal computer, which is supposed to be the center of the technological household, but we didn’t really get that. We got laptops that people mostly use at work and use a bit at home. Then we got mobile, and mobile is supposed to be the thing that you engage with when you leave your house on your way to work. Of course, the fundamental media of mobile is so addicting that it’s all-consuming. We use it at work, we use it at home — we use it all the time. But my observation about our use of it in the home is that nobody loves it. No spouse has ever said, “I wish my husband was on his phone more. I wish my kid used their iPad more,” and so we’re looking for ways to get beyond that. To your point, the other compute that’s in the home, like I said, is the set-top box, which is largely just a web browser to a bunch of services that live in the cloud. I think it’s pretty interesting, actually, that in 17 million homes Sonos is an actual mesh of compute in your house with real horsepower, real memory, real CPU, real capability, a real operating system — all just waiting to be the container for some of the kinds of things you’re talking about. So it’s super interesting. We’ll figure it out over time. I feel like you’re this close to being like, “And then the Teslas will be a data center.” There’s something there that is maybe the line. Actually, I want to talk about that. I actually want to push on that a little bit. The initial Sonos innovation 100 years ago, when the company started, was, “Oh, we can build a mesh network. We can do wireless audio at scale. We can synchronize the latency of all the speakers so it sounds like the same music playing at the same time.” This was a lot of big engineering back in the day. Still, I mean, candidly, still. A lot of what our software team does day in and day out is extend and maintain that infrastructure. There are features you’re announcing here as part of Sonos Fabric that I think are interesting. If you have surrounds, you can just place them, and they’ll figure out that they’re surrounds and immediately start being the surround speakers in a home theater. There’s just a lot of potential, as you’re describing, in the notion that, “Oh, there’s a big network of small computers in my house that can come together and do things you would not expect.” Is your focus that they will always do audio things? Or is it the focus that they will have many more capabilities? I think any thoughtful product leader is going to tell you the focus is an important part of success. I do feel like there’s so much interesting work for us to do around creating an audio system that sets the mood for your home that I don’t want us to take our eye off of that opportunity. We are doing some really exciting things in Sonos Fabric and Sonos 27 that we should talk about, that get to some of the work that you’re describing. But certainly in the moments where you allow yourself to think about what the company is in five years and what it will be in 10 years, you can’t help but interrogate what the opportunity is for a mesh — a fabric of compute that lives in the home. I want to end by talking about headphones really quickly. We just had the CEO of Bose on. She and I had a pretty searching conversation about what happens to the headphone market in the time of AI wearables. My fear, my anxiety, about audio is always that consumers will always pick convenience over quality. It’s just the history of the… I’ve got a set of AirPods on this desk, and they don’t sound great, but boy, are they convenient. And that’s just the way it goes. It has always been what the market has demanded: convenience over quality. We’re going to enter a time when Apple puts cameras on AirPods, and you can talk to them with Siri. When Google and Samsung ship very similar products, there’s undoubtedly going to be a flood of AI hardware startups that want to put something in your ears or in your body in some way. You are in the headphone market. You’re talking a lot about AI; you’re talking a lot about Fabric. That seems like a cataclysm coming for headphones. The same way that the removal of the headphone jack was a cataclysm in the headphone market, this seems like the next one. How are you preparing for that? Do you think there’s going to be a range of voice assistants on headphones, or do you think what you would call the first-party vendors are going to just grab more and more of that share? Before we jump to the hypotheticals about where headphones are, can I tell you a little bit about the new headphones? Yeah, of course. All right. So one of the things that you get from entering a new market is the opportunity to build something and put it in customers’ homes and learn a lot about what matters and what doesn’t matter. So we launched Sonos Ace two years ago. I think measured against any of the other premium over-the-ear noise-canceling headphones in the market, they’re a great product. They’ve got great reviews; they have great noise cancelling. They’re super comfortable, and they look great. We’re really proud of the product, but they weren’t thoughtfully integrated into the Sonos ecosystem. I mean, at launch you could swap to one of our soundbars, not even all of our soundbars. I think it was the most visible expression of the missed opportunity of that moment for the company to always remember that the products that we make are part of the Sonos system, not individual offerings. So we ended up with a great pair of headphones, but honestly, I mean, you review them all the time; there are lots of great headphones. When we set out to take all the lessons that we learned from Ace to design Ace Ultra, at the very top of that list is that we have to do the hard thing. These headphones have to be able to show up in your home as a part of the system, and the model through which you invoke your headphones has to be completely seamless and delightful. We built an entirely new hardware platform for Ace Ultra called Headphone Engine 2, and it unlocks this capability at the hardware level. And then in Sonos OS 27, we built virtualization so that any one of the speakers in your home can deliver the audio platform to that speaker but can also act as a proxy for your headphones, which don’t have the horsepower to run the full stack — it would kill battery life, et cetera. Now with Ace Ultra, you’ll be able to link your headphones to your Sonos system, walk up to a speaker that’s playing, press a button on your headphones, and the music will jump from the speaker into your headphones. No Bluetooth, no phone. You’ll be able to walk around your whole house, enjoy the music, come to another speaker, press the button again, and it will jump to that speaker using some BLA location-sensing stuff that we’ve developed. It’s super magical. It’s the one job that we had and didn’t deliver on with Ace. We’re really excited to get it out into the market. Analogous to that on the home theater side is, as you mentioned, that we’re making all of our portable speakers — Sonos Play, Sonos Move — capable of being rear channels for home theater. That sounds really easy. Maybe people will even be like, “Why wasn’t that always possible?” But to your point about the deep technology of it, the way that we achieve high-fidelity, low-latency surround experiences in the living room is by directly bonding our rear channel speakers and subwoofer to the soundbar on a proprietary network, not through your access point. So for a speaker to seamlessly hop between being part of your Sonos system as a music node and part of your Sonos system as a surround channel means that you have to do a real-time reconfiguration of that networking stack, and you have to know when to do it. We’re using accelerometers in the product to actually know that you’ve picked it up and set it down in a new location. We’re using Sonos’ positioning system, which is ultrasonic signaling, to broadcast to the room, “Hey, is there a soundbar here?” Ultrasonic comes back saying, “I’m here.” They negotiate position, left and right, and distance, so that they can optimize the surround sound experience. You pick it up again, you take it back to the kitchen, and it’s a regular speaker again. All happens magically, no use of the app. It’s pretty cool. Answer my question on headphones, though. This is my big worry. You’ve got really cool headphones. They have a feature that no one else can ship, and Apple’s going to say, “Look, our new AirPods have Siri AI in them.” You can just say, “Show me what I’m looking at,” and a picture will be taken automatically and something will happen. We’ll get over the privacy implications of that, but that’s a collapse of the headphone market. Maybe. I mean, headphones come in all kinds of form factors today: over-ear, in-ear, cuffs, wireless, wired. So I do think it’s a market where people choose different form factors for different tasks. We’re really focused on this personal in-the-home listening — what do you do when the baby’s asleep? What do you do when you want to move the party from the kitchen to the den while you relax for the evening? We think that there’s a bunch of really interesting use cases there that other people aren’t paying attention to. I think, broadly, over the course of the next couple of years, we’re going to get all kinds of adventurous wackadoodle consumer electronics that are connected to this new emerging AI universe. Most of them will be a swing and a miss. Of course, we’ve already seen some of those. So it’s a little hard to speculate, I think, about which of these things, if any, is going to have its iPod moment or its iPhone moment or whatever. What do you think is going to happen? I think we’re going to see a replay of what happened when the headphone jack got taken away. The headphone jack was an open interconnect. There was a really vibrant market for all kinds of headphones, and a bunch of those companies don’t exist anymore. The high-end wired headphones, for phones anyway, have mostly gone away, and you have a bunch of medium Bluetooth competitors, but the phone makers have largely taken that with first-party products. Now, you have your products at the high end competing with really high-end noise-canceling products from Bose and Sony and whoever, and that is the airplane set. The lack of the open interconnect has really killed the vibrancy of the low and middle end of the market. Okay, well, there’s one big thing they can do to make sure the high end belongs to them, and it’s to integrate AI in very specific ways directly into their operating system. We’ll see how that plays out. There’s also a thing that’s different this time: there’s a vastly more energized European regulatory environment. Who knows how this will play out? Sure. I can’t tell you, but all that stuff is a swirl, and you’re a headphone maker, and it seems like different headphone makers are taking different approaches to this. The only counter that I might offer is that there’s a lot of talk about the walled garden of the Bluetooth advantages that the platform companies have. But I would say even without the European regulators, it’s notable that something like the Meta Glasses can have a reasonable, I think, commercially viable set of experiences that are principally powered by compute that lives on your phone and still deliver conversational AI that is mediated by a Bluetooth connection, admittedly behind some of the obstacles that you’re describing. But those obstacles aren’t so profound that clever companies aren’t figuring out how to work within those constraints. I’m very curious to see how that plays out. It doesn’t seem like it’s in focus. Again, probably because, as you say, none of the products are in focus. No one knows what a hit product here looks like, so you might as well let a thousand flowers bloom and then radically constrict the market. Yeah, sure. Tom, I’ve burned just a ton of your time. I think you can tell I could talk to you for ages and ages about all kinds of things. Super fun. Tell us what’s next for Sonos. When does all this stuff ship? So I think by the time this airs, we’ll have announced all of this to the world. We’re having a big event in New York to share Sonos OS 27, Sonos Voice 27, and the Ace Ultra and Beam Ultra. We can’t wait to get this stuff out into the world and begin to hear what our customers do with all of these exciting new products. Many of the software features are going to be available in early access, which will mean our customers will opt into them, be able to give us feedback, and we’ll be able to observe the telemetry that comes back from their homes and make sure that we’re delivering exactly the experience that we want. We’re excited about the moment of co-creation that’s around the corner for us. As we talked about at the top of the hour, Sonos 27 is absolutely a nod to the fact that we intend to keep doing this until the sun burns out. There’ll be Sonos 28 and 29 and 30 and beyond. That’s great. All right, I’ve got to ask you at the end: I have ceiling speakers in my kitchen. They’re connected to a Sonos Amp. There’s a Google Home Hub right there, and it’s broken. I can’t ask it to play music in the kitchen. When are you going to fix that for me? I’m ending on tech support. All right. I don’t know the answer, but I’d love to figure it out for you. I know the right folks to call, so let’s get you connected. We’re going to have a Decoder roundtable. If your listeners have similar kinds of problems, we’ve got great people to help them, and we always like to hear from you. You can find me on social pretty easily. Usually I end by inviting people back, but I’m saying we’ve got to fix it, and then we’re going to talk about what it took to fix it. That’s the plan. All right. Right on. Tom, this is great. Thank you so much, man. This was super fun. Thank you. Questions or comments? Hit us up at decoder@theverge.com. We really do read every email! ]]>
paragraphs: Today, I’m talking with Tom Conrad, the CEO of Sonos. Tom and I have known each other for a long time — he was the chief technology officer of Pandora, VP of product at Snap, and the chief product officer of Quibi. He was also on the board at Sonos during its disastrous 2024 app redesign that threatened to crash the entire brand.

Tom took over as interim CEO to right the ship during that period, and then took the permanent role just about a year ago. As you’ll hear him say, he thinks Sonos is fully out of that period now, and on to its next chapter with a huge product and platform launch called Sonos 27 .

I mean, come on, you all listen to the show. That is all the most Decoder bait imaginable. I have been dying to have Tom on the show to talk about how the board decided to move on from previous CEO Patrick Spence, how he diagnosed the issues inside the company, and what decisions he made to fix them.

Those fixes involved a lot of big changes: to the company’s structure, its product lineup, and how it thinks about itself and what its product fundamentally is. That’s that new platform, Sonos 27, which you’ll hear Tom call a new foundation for the company that makes every Sonos product work better as part of a system.

There’s a lot here, including how AI assistants can work across the system, the idea of having a mesh network of little computers in your home disguised as speakers, and of course, the testy relationship between Sonos and Google, which means Google’s Gemini assistant isn’t available on Sonos devices.

article.title: Apple gặp rắc rối với iPhone Ultra trước ngày ra mắt?
article.summary: Cụ thể, sản lượng iPhone Ultra chỉ đạt vài trăm chiếc mỗi ngày vào cuối tháng 8, trong khi Apple cần sản xuất hàng chục nghìn chiếc mỗi ngày để đáp ứng nhu cầu. Mặc dù Apple và các nhà cung cấp đang nỗ lực tăng cường sản xuất, nhưng quá trình này có thể mất thời gian.
article.dek: Cụ thể, sản lượng iPhone Ultra chỉ đạt vài trăm chiếc mỗi ngày vào cuối tháng 8, trong khi Apple cần sản xuất hàng chục nghìn chiếc mỗi ngày để đáp ứng nhu cầu.
article.hook: Cụ thể, sản lượng iPhone Ultra chỉ đạt vài trăm chiếc mỗi ngày vào cuối tháng 8, trong khi Apple cần sản xuất hàng chục nghìn chiếc mỗi ngày để đáp ứng nhu cầu.

sections.heading: Bối cảnh: điều gì đang đổi
sections.body: Cụ thể, sản lượng iPhone Ultra chỉ đạt vài trăm chiếc mỗi ngày vào cuối tháng 8, trong khi Apple cần sản xuất hàng chục nghìn chiếc mỗi ngày để đáp ứng nhu cầu. Mặc dù Apple và các nhà cung cấp đang nỗ lực tăng cường sản xuất, nhưng quá trình này có thể mất thời gian. Nếu tình hình không cải thiện nhanh chóng, việc sở hữu iPhone Ultra sẽ trở nên khó khăn, đặc biệt trong những tuần đầu sau khi ra mắt.

sections.heading: Các nguồn đang khớp nhau ở đâu
sections.body: Tiêu chuẩn cao của Apple dành cho iPhone Ultra đang làm khó các đối tác sản xuất.

sections.heading: Tác động thực tế với người đọc
sections.body: Nguyên nhân chính dẫn đến sản lượng thấp là do tiêu chuẩn kiểm soát chất lượng cao mà Apple đang áp dụng. Công ty đã tiến hành thêm một đợt chạy thử và quy trình kiểm tra xác thực vào tháng 8, làm chậm quá trình sản xuất thương mại. Hai yếu tố quan trọng mà Apple chú trọng là hiệu suất bản lề và độ phẳng của màn hình, vốn yêu cầu thử nghiệm trong điều kiện khắc nghiệt hơn so với các đối thủ.

sections.heading: Ai nên chú ý lúc này
sections.body: Ban đầu, Apple đặt mục tiêu bán khoảng 7 - 8 triệu chiếc iPhone Ultra trước khi kết thúc năm 2026, sau đó nâng lên khoảng 10 triệu chiếc. Tuy nhiên, với sản lượng thấp như hiện nay, mục tiêu của Apple có thể gặp thách thức. Hơn nữa, iPhone Ultra cần thêm thời gian để đánh giá độ bền, điều mà Galaxy Z Fold8 đang có nhiều lợi thế.

sections.heading: Điều cần theo dõi tiếp
sections.body: Việc Apple cần thêm các bước kiểm soát chất lượng iPhone Ultra được cho là bắt nguồn từ các trục trặc sản xuất và vấn đề nguồn cung. Công ty đã gặp phải nhiều khó khăn với vật liệu bản lề, thậm chí dẫn đến việc điện thoại phát ra tiếng lạch cạch. Những trở ngại này có thể khiến lịch trình ra mắt của iPhone Ultra khác biệt hoàn toàn so với iPhone 18 Pro và 18 Pro Max. Mặc dù không trì hoãn ngày giới thiệu, nhưng có khả năng việc đặt trước và giao hàng sẽ bị trì hoãn đến cuối tháng 10 hoặc đầu tháng 11 giống như những gì mà iPhone X đã gặp vào năm 2017, thậm chí một số nguồn tin còn cho rằng việc ra mắt iPhone Ultra có thể bị đẩy lùi đến mùa xuân năm sau.

draft_context.source_title: Apple gặp rắc rối với iPhone Ultra trước ngày ra mắt?
draft_context.description: Chiếc iPhone màn hình gập đầu tiên của Apple đang gặp vấn đề sản xuất nghiêm trọng, khiến nguồn cung ban đầu có thể rất hạn chế.
paragraphs: Cụ thể, sản lượng iPhone Ultra chỉ đạt vài trăm chiếc mỗi ngày vào cuối tháng 8, trong khi Apple cần sản xuất hàng chục nghìn chiếc mỗi ngày để đáp ứng nhu cầu. Mặc dù Apple và các nhà cung cấp đang nỗ lực tăng cường sản xuất, nhưng quá trình này có thể mất thời gian. Nếu tình hình không cải thiện nhanh chóng, việc sở hữu iPhone Ultra sẽ trở nên khó khăn, đặc biệt trong những tuần đầu sau khi ra mắt.
Tiêu chuẩn cao của Apple dành cho iPhone Ultra đang làm khó các đối tác sản xuất

Nguyên nhân chính dẫn đến sản lượng thấp là do tiêu chuẩn kiểm soát chất lượng cao mà Apple đang áp dụng. Công ty đã tiến hành thêm một đợt chạy thử và quy trình kiểm tra xác thực vào tháng 8, làm chậm quá trình sản xuất thương mại. Hai yếu tố quan trọng mà Apple chú trọng là hiệu suất bản lề và độ phẳng của màn hình, vốn yêu cầu thử nghiệm trong điều kiện khắc nghiệt hơn so với các đối thủ.

Ban đầu, Apple đặt mục tiêu bán khoảng 7 - 8 triệu chiếc iPhone Ultra trước khi kết thúc năm 2026, sau đó nâng lên khoảng 10 triệu chiếc. Tuy nhiên, với sản lượng thấp như hiện nay, mục tiêu của Apple có thể gặp thách thức. Hơn nữa, iPhone Ultra cần thêm thời gian để đánh giá độ bền, điều mà Galaxy Z Fold8 đang có nhiều lợi thế.

Việc Apple cần thêm các bước kiểm soát chất lượng iPhone Ultra được cho là bắt nguồn từ các trục trặc sản xuất và vấn đề nguồn cung. Công ty đã gặp phải nhiều khó khăn với vật liệu bản lề, thậm chí dẫn đến việc điện thoại phát ra tiếng lạch cạch. Những trở ngại này có thể khiến lịch trình ra mắt của iPhone Ultra khác biệt hoàn toàn so với iPhone 18 Pro và 18 Pro Max. Mặc dù không trì hoãn ngày giới thiệu, nhưng có khả năng việc đặt trước và giao hàng sẽ bị trì hoãn đến cuối tháng 10 hoặc đầu tháng 11 giống như những gì mà iPhone X đã gặp vào năm 2017, thậm chí một số nguồn tin còn cho rằng việc ra mắt iPhone Ultra có thể bị đẩy lùi đến mùa xuân năm sau.

Sự chậm trễ này có thể mang lại lợi thế cho các đối thủ cạnh tranh của Apple, như Samsung, Huawei và Xiaomi, khi họ có thêm thời gian để chiếm lĩnh thị trường. Việc trì hoãn kéo dài là điều không thể chấp nhận và người tiêu dùng sẽ đánh giá cao một chiếc điện thoại gập bền bỉ, đặc biệt nếu nó có giá cả phải chăng. Apple cần duy trì truyền thống ra mắt sản phẩm ngay sau khi công bố, đặc biệt với một sản phẩm mới như iPhone Ultra. Tuy nhiên, nhiều người có thể sẵn lòng chờ đợi thêm một thời gian, nhất là khi Apple đã chậm chân trong lĩnh vực smartphone gập gần một thế kỷ.

article.title: Cơn ác mộng giá RAM sẽ không biến mất trước khi GTA VI lên PC
article.summary: Rockstar Games vừa phát hành video GTA VI: An Extended Look, mang đến cái nhìn rõ hơn về thế giới, nhân vật và lối chơi của bom tấn được chờ đợi suốt nhiều năm. Game dự kiến ra mắt trên PS5 và Xbox Series X|S vào ngày 19/11/2026, còn phiên bản PC vẫn chưa được công bố lịch phát hành.

sections.body: Nếu Rockstar tiếp tục cách phát hành quen thuộc, game thủ PC có thể phải chờ thêm ít nhất một năm. GTA V lên máy tính khoảng 19 tháng sau bản console, trong khi Red Dead Redemption 2 cũng mất hơn một năm để thực hiện hành trình tương tự.

sections.heading: Tác động thực tế với người đọc
sections.body: Thế nhưng đến lúc GTA VI đặt chân lên PC, người chơi có thể vẫn chưa thoát khỏi một vấn đề khác là giá bộ nhớ. draft_context.source_title: Cơn ác mộng giá RAM sẽ không biến mất trước khi GTA VI lên PC
draft_context.description: Video mới của GTA VI khiến cộng đồng háo hức, nhưng game thủ PC vẫn còn một cuộc chờ khác. Đến khi bom tấn này xuất hiện trên máy tính, thị trường bộ nhớ có thể vẫn chưa trở lại bình thường.
paragraphs: Rockstar Games vừa phát hành video GTA VI: An Extended Look, mang đến cái nhìn rõ hơn về thế giới, nhân vật và lối chơi của bom tấn được chờ đợi suốt nhiều năm. Game dự kiến ra mắt trên PS5 và Xbox Series X|S vào ngày 19/11/2026, còn phiên bản PC vẫn chưa được công bố lịch phát hành.

Nếu Rockstar tiếp tục cách phát hành quen thuộc, game thủ PC có thể phải chờ thêm ít nhất một năm. GTA V lên máy tính khoảng 19 tháng sau bản console, trong khi Red Dead Redemption 2 cũng mất hơn một năm để thực hiện hành trình tương tự.

Thế nhưng đến lúc GTA VI đặt chân lên PC, người chơi có thể vẫn chưa thoát khỏi một vấn đề khác là giá bộ nhớ. draft_context.source_title: Tim Cook kết thúc chặng đường huy hoàng trên ghế CEO Apple
draft_context.description: Ngày 31/8, Tim Cook rời vị trí CEO Apple , khép lại 15 năm lãnh đạo tập đoàn công nghệ Mỹ. Người kế nhiệm ông là John Ternus, Phó Chủ tịch cấp cao phụ trách kỹ thuật phần cứng của Apple. Tim Cook sẽ tiếp tục làm việc tại Apple với vai trò Chủ tịch điều hành và hỗ trợ công ty trong một số lĩnh vực, trong đó có làm việc với các nhà hoạch định chính sách trên toàn thế giới, theo thông báo của hãng “Táo khuyết”. Trong thời gian giữ chức CEO, Tim Cook đã giám sát quá trình Apple ra mắt nhiều sản phẩm mới, trong đó có Apple Watch, AirPods và gần đây là MacBook Neo. Ông cũng đóng vai trò quan trọng trong việc đưa doanh thu mảng Dịch vụ của Apple vượt mốc 100 tỷ USD, trở thành mảng kinh doanh lớn thứ hai của công ty, chỉ sau iPhone. CEO Tim Cook khi đến thăm Việt Nam năm 2024. (Ảnh: Mạnh Hùng) Steve Jobs tuyển Tim Cook vào Apple năm 1998 và bổ nhiệm ông làm Phó Chủ tịch điều hành phụ trách bán hàng toàn cầu năm 2002, trước khi đưa ông lên vị trí Giám đốc vận hành (COO) vào năm 2005. Năm 2011, Tim Cook kế nhiệm Steve Jobs và trở thành CEO Apple. Trong thời gian lãnh đạo, vị CEO này tận dụng kinh nghiệm về chuỗi cung ứng để mở rộng đáng kể hoạt động kinh doanh của Apple. Vốn hóa thị trường của công ty tăng từ khoảng 350 tỷ USD lên hơn 4.000 tỷ USD, tương đương mức tăng khoảng 1.000%. Doanh thu hàng năm của Apple tăng mạnh, từ 108 tỷ USD năm 2011 lên 416 tỷ USD năm 2025. Riêng doanh thu iPhone tăng mạnh từ 47,1 tỷ USD lên 209,6 tỷ USD trong cùng giai đoạn. CEO Apple Tim Cook. (Ảnh: Getty) Apple Watch và AirPods cũng trở thành những sản phẩm đồng hồ thông minh và tai nghe phổ biến nhất thế giới. Một dấu ấn quan trọng khác của Tim Cook là thúc đẩy Apple chuyển từ chip Intel sang chip do hãng tự thiết kế cho dòng máy Mac. Việc tự phát triển chip giúp cải thiện đáng kể hiệu năng máy tính, đồng thời mang lại thời lượng pin vượt trội, lợi thế mà các đối thủ chỉ mới bắt kịp trong những năm gần đây. John Ternus tiếp quản vị trí CEO Apple trong bối cảnh công ty đang bước vào giai đoạn chuyển đổi lớn. Apple đang nỗ lực cải thiện năng lực trí tuệ nhân tạo (AI) sau khi được cho là chậm chân hơn các đối thủ như Microsoft và Google. John Ternus và Tim Cook tại Apple Park. (Ảnh: Apple) Apple được kỳ vọng ra mắt phiên bản Siri mới sử dụng các mô hình AI Gemini của Google tại Hội nghị các nhà phát triển toàn cầu (WWDC) vào tháng 6. Bên cạnh đó, Apple được cho là đang chuẩn bị một trong những thay đổi lớn nhất đối với iPhone, với mẫu iPhone màn hình gập dự kiến ra mắt không lâu sau khi Tim Cook rời ghế CEO. Dưới thời Ternus, Apple cũng có thể trình làng kính thông minh và các sản phẩm tập trung vào AI nhằm cạnh tranh với những thiết bị AI thế hệ mới, trong đó có sản phẩm được OpenAI định hướng phát triển theo mô hình “AI-first”. Chặng đường mới của Apple dưới sự lãnh đạo của John Ternus sẽ chính thức bắt đầu từ ngày 1/9. Apple chuẩn bị sự kiện iPhone khác lạ nhất trong nhiều năm VOV.VN - Apple đã chốt ngày ra mắt iPhone mới, nhưng kế hoạch được cho là sẽ phá vỡ truyền thống giới thiệu toàn bộ dòng máy.

article.title: Con người nằm ở đâu trong vòng lặp bảo mật “có" AI?
article.summary: Sáng 05/08/2026, sự kiện BSides Hanoi lần thứ 2 chính thức diễn ra tại Hà Nội để tìm ra câu trả lời về mối quan hệ giữa con người và AI trong hệ thống bảo mật thời số hoá. Ông Vũ Duy Hiền, Phó Tổng thư ký kiêm Chánh Văn phòng Hiệp hội An ninh mạng Quốc gia phát biểu tại sự kiện.

sections.heading: Tác động thực tế với người đọc
sections.body: BSides Hanoi 2026 lần thứ 2 tổ chức tại Hà Nội với chủ đề "No Human", diễn ra trong tuần lễ chào mừng Ngày An ninh mạng Việt Nam 06/08. Chương trình năm nay trải rộng trên nhiều chủ đề, từ bảo mật blockchain, điều tra số trong kỷ nguyên Apple Intelligence, hoạt động của các nhóm tấn công có chủ đích (APT), phân tích mã độc, threat intelligence đến ứng dụng AI trong nghiên cứu và phòng thủ. Mỗi nghiên cứu tiếp cận một lát cắt khác nhau, nhưng khi đặt cạnh nhau lại phản ánh những chuyển dịch đang định hình an ninh mạng hiện đại.

sections.heading: Ai nên chú ý lúc này
sections.body: Điểm chung đầu tiên là AI đang làm thay đổi cán cân giữa bên tấn công và bên phòng thủ. Những công nghệ giúp chuyên gia tăng tốc phân tích, tự động hóa quy trình và phát hiện mối đe dọa cũng đang được các nhóm tấn công khai thác để gia tăng tốc độ, quy mô và mức độ tinh vi của các chiến dịch. Cuộc cạnh tranh vì thế không còn nằm ở việc ai sở hữu AI, mà ở khả năng khai thác, kiểm soát và sử dụng AI hiệu quả hơn.

sections.heading: Điều cần theo dõi tiếp
sections.body: Được tổ chức bởi Công ty CP An ninh mạng Việt Nam (VSEC - thành viên của Tập đoàn Công nghệ G-Group), phối hợp cùng Hiệp hội An ninh mạng quốc gia (NCA) và Hiệp hội Internet Việt Nam (VIA), sự kiện tiếp tục mang tinh thần của chuỗi BSides toàn cầu – một diễn đàn cộng đồng, nơi các nhà nghiên cứu và chuyên gia chia sẻ nghiên cứu thực tiễn, phản biện các xu hướng mới và cùng tìm lời giải cho những thách thức của ngành.

Được tổ chức bởi Công ty CP An ninh mạng Việt Nam (VSEC - thành viên của Tập đoàn Công nghệ G-Group), phối hợp cùng Hiệp hội An ninh mạng quốc gia (NCA) và Hiệp hội Internet Việt Nam (VIA), sự kiện tiếp tục mang tinh thần của chuỗi BSides toàn cầu – một diễn đàn cộng đồng, nơi các nhà nghiên cứu và chuyên gia chia sẻ nghiên cứu thực tiễn, phản biện các xu hướng mới và cùng tìm lời giải cho những thách thức của ngành.

Theo ông Trương Đức Lượng, Chủ tịch HĐQT VSEC và thành viên Hội đồng Chuyên môn, BSides được xây dựng như một nền tảng để kết nối cộng đồng bảo mật Việt Nam với cộng đồng quốc tế, khuyến khích chia sẻ tri thức và thúc đẩy sự phát triển bền vững của hệ sinh thái an ninh mạng.

draft_context.source_title: The rumored folding iPhone Ultra looks sick, but Android foldables offer something more: choice
draft_context.description: Rumor has it that Apple will announce the iPhone Ultra at its upcoming September 9 event, making it the first iPhone to sport an "ultra" moniker. We're not expecting it to push the boundaries of battery technology or camera prowess, but it is slated to do one big thing that no other iPhone has (intentionally) done: fold in half. This is going to drive a huge boost in sales for foldable phones , a category that has consistently grown since the first models arrived in 2019, but hasn't seen a particularly massive tentpole release like this one yet. Of course, as with anything Apple makes, you'll only get what Apple gives you, and rumor has it that Apple is announcing only one size and shape this time around. But Android foldables, which have been around for eight years now, have had time to develop and branch out. Android offers a substantial choice of manufacturers, shapes, sizes, and capabilities that Apple simply can't offer. If foldable phones are looking like your next big purchase, here are many reasons you should choose an Android-powered one. What is a folding phone and how do they work? (Image credit: Derrek Lee / Android Central) Folding phones usually come with two displays: an inner display and an outer display. The inner display is made of special ultrathin glass that can bend (unlike normal glass) and is reinforced with a preinstalled screen protector. The phone's frame is split into two halves connected by a specialized hinge, allowing you to open and close the phone. The foldable inner display is a special type of flexible OLED panel that's built to bend, too. A specialized hinge holds everything together, keeping dust and water out of the phone. It's a true marvel of engineering, and some foldables are even extremely durable, as proven by my Honor Magic V6 torture test . Both the inner and outer displays work the same way a regular smartphone touchscreen does. You can open apps on either of them, allowing you to choose the size of the "canvas" you want to view them on. What types of folding phones exist (and why would someone want one)? The rumored iPhone Ultra. (Image credit: AppleTrack) The leaked image of the iPhone Ultra above shows what's known as a book-style foldable. When a book-style phone is closed, its size and shape are similar to those of a standard smartphone, so all your favorite apps look and feel nearly identical to those on your existing smartphone. Opening a book-style phone doubles its size, turning it into a small tablet that lets you get more done without switching to a laptop or other computer. I work on the go quite a bit, and a folding phone makes it easy to get most of my work done efficiently. I rarely watch videos on my phone, but when I do, the extra-large inner display is a real treat. Because of the large size, multitasking is one of the best features of a book-style foldable. You can run two or three apps side by side on these phones, and even put apps in floating windows, like on a laptop OS. Plus, the taskbar on the inner display makes it feel even more like a multitasking beast, similar to a laptop OS (like Windows or macOS). Book-style foldables come in many sizes and shapes, though most are slightly taller and narrower than your average smartphone when closed. Google began its foldable journey with a shorter, wider model , but made the next three entries a bit taller. Meanwhile, Samsung just introduced its first shorter, wider model (the Galaxy Z Fold 8 ), and Apple's iPhone Ultra is rumored to use this same size and shape. Shorter, wider models are best for video content and feel a lot like holding a small TV when unfolded. Apple's iPhone Ultra is said to come in just one shape and size, while Android foldables offer tons of different sizes, shapes, and form factors. You can even get tri-fold foldables ! (Image credit: Android Central) While book-style foldables get the bulk of the attention, flip-style foldables were better sellers for a few years. Phones like the Motorola Razr 2026 series look like a slightly taller normal smartphone when opened, then fold into a perfectly pocketable half-sized phone when closed. These phones solve the issue of overly large phones while still giving you the flexibility to use a small screen for things like notifications and messaging, then a larger screen when you need it. We generally recommend Motorola's Razr flip phones over Samsung's Z Flip line because Motorola's outer screen is more capable , and the company's designs are far more interesting. Flip phones are also wonderful for photos and videos thanks to their shape. It's easy to bend a flip phone at a 90-degree angle and use it as a "tripod" to take group photos. You can also use this same shape and hold it sideways to take video like a classic camcorder. Do folding phones have any downsides? (Image credit: Nicholas Sutrich) Folding phones offer unique form factors and ways to interact with your favorite apps, but not everything is a win-win. When shopping for a book-style folding phone, the first thing you'll probably notice is the price. Yeah, there's quite a bit of sticker shock here, and that's mainly because this is a two-in-one device. Think of it as buying a phone and a tablet at the same time, and you'll understand. Flip-style phones are typically priced the same as traditional flagship phones but tend to have one fewer rear camera. Even Motorola's Razr Ultra line doesn't have a third camera on the back, despite the higher price. Both flip and book-style foldables are often a bit less powerful than top-tier traditional flagship smartphones. The problem is that there's not as much space in these phones for cooling, since they have to be thinner than a traditional phone to avoid feeling like a brick when closed. (Image credit: Nicholas Sutrich / Android Central) Lastly, durability. Folding phones got a bad rap pretty early on when the original Galaxy Z Fold's inner display would spontaneously break, but those problems have generally been solved. There's always a chance the folding glass could break, but these phones have undergone so many years of evolution and hardening that such a failure is almost unheard of. Stores like uBreakiFix readily have parts to repair them, and phone companies offer warranties and other insurance programs that help cover any potential issues. As someone who has reviewed dozens and dozens of folding phones over the past seven years, I've never seen a phone break in person. My wife has also been using flip phones for the past four years, and the only time one of hers broke was after being dropped with the phone unfolded. Considering how many traditional smartphones break every day from drops, there's no reason to suggest that these phones are any less durable with regular use. ]]>

draft_context.source_title: Get ready, Apple’s iPhone event is massive this year
draft_context.description: Macworld Apple always holds its events at 10 am PT, with iPhone launches usually taking place on the second Tuesday or Wednesday of September. This year, that means the event, dubbed Surprise and Shine , will take place on Wednesday, September 9. Additionally, Apple always introduces its new iPhones and Apple Watches at its September special event, and this year is no different. Except this year, everything is different. The iPhones are different . The CEO is different . The event may be different. Here’s what we expect from Apple’s big September show. The John Ternus show Tim Cook stepped down from his position as CEO after 15 years, though he will remain on the board of directors. He has named John Ternus, who was most recently senior vice president of hardware engineering, as his successor. That means this is the first Apple Special Event in which Ternus will be the headliner, introducing the start of the event and thanking everyone at the end. Individual products are likely to be demonstrated by other Apple executives—they always are—but this is a big opportunity to shake up the format of Apple events in general. Will we see a return to live stage events ? Will the structure and format of the pre-recorded video events change at all? Or will Ternus be essentially interchangeable for Tim Cook, with nothing else about these big product reveals changing at all? Will Apple make a “Turn” pun at some point? We’ll have to wait and see. iPhone Ultra For the first time in over a decade, Apple is going to dramatically change the iPhone’s form factor. Apple is going to release a folding iPhone, which most are expecting to be called iPhone Ultra. It will fold in half like a book and be shaped sort of like a passport when closed; an unusual aspect ratio for any phone and especially an iPhone. This should be the relative size and shape of the folding iPhone Ultra. Foundry We expect two cameras (wide and ultrawide) on the back, one on the front, and the reintroduction of Touch ID in the side button for authentication. This is going to be a very premium product, with most rumors citing a starting price of $2,000 or more. Not much is known about the software experience, though. Obviously, Apple will need to change some of how iOS looks and feels, and offer impressive new software features, to justify a folding phone with displays on the outside and inside and all new aspect ratios and sizes. Check out our roundup of rumors about the iPhone Ultra for more. iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max The iPhone Ultra won’t be the only high-priced iPhone hitting the market this fall. With the standard iPhone 18 supposedly getting bumped back to a spring release, the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max are going to be the only other iPhones launched this fall. We expect an upgraded A20 Pro processor , a better modem (the C2 in many countries, possibly a Qualcomm modem in the U.S.), and a new Dark Cherry signature color . A dark red/cherry color should be the signature shade of the iPhone 18 Pro, along with Light Blue, Dark Gray, and Silver. Foundry For the most part, the iPhone 18 Pro will resemble the iPhone 17 Pro, but there should be a big upgrade to the rear camera (variable aperture, new sensor technology) and possibly a boost to 24 megapixels for the front camera. Battery capacity may go up by 6-8 percent, which could lead to longer battery life in conjunction with other improvements and optimizations. Check out our roundup of rumors about the iPhone 18 Pro for more. Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 Apple always updates its Apple Watch line at the same time as the iPhone, whether it needs to or not. That means that this year, we’ll see the Apple Watch Series 12 and the Ultra 4. So far, none of the rumors suggest much of a change from the previous model. There will be a somewhat faster S12 processor, but major new health features or other changes don’t seem to be in the cards this year. Rumors say there won’t be a new SE 4 this year. Apple TV and Homepod mini Both long overdue for an update, Apple has been waiting to release a new Apple TV 4K set-top box and the HomePod mini until it figured out how to really make the new Siri work. Now, with a whole new Siri architecture coming in the OS 27 updates this fall, it’s finally ready to ship these products. Because Apple TV set-top boxes and HomePods act as a “home hub” for Apple’s smart home controls, Apple needed to make sure they’re capable of running the all-new Siri. That said, we haven’t heard of any major new software features that make use of the improved hardware coming to Apple TV or HomePod. These new products will give you the new Siri experience just as a modern Apple Watch will, but the tvOS interface and features probably won’t get a big change. It’s more like: you’ll ask Siri something, and you’ll get Siri AI answers, not the old Siri. Foundry HomePad preview The new Apple TV and HomePod mini will mark the start of a bigger, more ambitious smart home plan for Apple that all revolves around the new Siri and the expanded AI features that will be built out on top of it in the coming months and years. The main device we’re waiting for is the so-called HomePad smart hub that has long been rumored. The device is expected to have an iPad-like squarish screen that can either hang on a wall or dock to a speaker. It will reportedly run a new operating system dubbed HomeOS that is powered by Siri AI. In his August 9 Power On newsletter , Mark Gurman reported that “a September preview of that product is plausible.” That could very well be Ternus’ surprise “One more Thing” to close the show. However, it is unlikely to go on sale until later in 2026 or early 2027.

draft_context.source_title: 'Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 2' PC remote code exploits have been fixed, says Activision
draft_context.description: I've been following this story for a while, but it seems like Call of Duty fans of at least one of their PC versions have cause to celebrate this week. Microsoft has been hard at work leveraging its Call of Duty acquisition to boost Xbox's fortunes in recent years, shipping Black Ops 1 and 2 "classic" versions exclusively onto PlayStation to huge fanfare. Indeed, the "classic" Call of Duty versions have been in the spotlight somewhat lately, as fans clamor for an era of a more grounded, less microtransaction-laden Call of Duty. Modern versions are replete with pop culture bloat and mountains of "features" nobody really asked for, leaving nostalgic millennials and older gen-z players yearning for simpler times. Of course, you can always play the classic Call of Duty games on PC via Steam or on Xbox Series X|S via backwards compatibility. The downside is that these classic Call of Duty versions are often infested with aimbot hackers at best, and RCE vulnerabilities at worst . Remote Code Execution (RCE) exploits allow players in multiplayer titles to literally upload malware to your computer. The way some older games work with regard to peer-to-peer networking, if left unpatched, facilitate this malignant type of attack. Modern Warfare 2 on PC has been notorious for these types of vulnerabilities unfortunately, but there may be light at the end of the tunnel. In a statement to Windows Central, Activision claimed the following: " An update released this week addressed all known vulnerabilities in Modern Warfare 2. The team continues to support our legacy titles, with additional updates coming soon. We encourage anyone aware of additional issues to report them through Activision's Bug Bounty Portal ." There are other reports of aimbots, wall hacks, and even RCE exploits in other classic Call of Duty PC games, but it sounds as though Activision is now actively working through these after realizing the potential goldmine it's sitting on. Indeed, Call of Duty: Black Ops 1 and 2 dominated the PlayStation store over the summer, potentially opening up new revenue streams for the legendary franchise. What about Call of Duty on Xbox backwards compatibility? Classic Call of Duty games are available on Xbox backwards compatibility ... but it's a double edged sword somewhat. (Image credit: Activision) I've also requested for Activision to comment on the Xbox backwards compatible versions of Call of Duty, which are similarly replete with hackers and aimbots and the like. Xbox backwards compatibility is one of the best features Xbox Series X|S and Xbox One have in my view. It allows hundreds of classic Xbox and Xbox 360 games to carry forward, ensuring that your purchases travel with you. In the early days, having all of the classic Call of Duty titles in one place is arguably a huge selling point for Xbox as a console ecosystem. However, Microsoft itself offered a huge flaw in the system this summer, when it ported the classic Black Ops 1 and 2 exclusively to PlayStation, complete with modernized security updates and server infrastructure. It's a sad state of affairs for Xbox fans of classic Call of Duty games potentially. Despite Xbox literally owning Call of Duty, Xbox fans are left with the worst experience thanks to the unpatched security vulnerabilities. Since the classic Call of Duty titles available on Xbox Series X|S today are effectively Xbox 360 versions, the source code of which is likely archived, it seems incredibly unlikely Microsoft and Activision will be willing to patch some of these. The Xbox 360 security layers are easily bypassed these days, with modded consoles opening up old school backwards compatible multiplayer titles to a variety of vulnerabilities. It's a sad state of affairs for Xbox fans of classic Call of Duty games potentially. Despite Xbox literally owning Call of Duty, Xbox fans are left with the worst experience thanks to the unpatched security vulnerabilities. I'll update this article if Activision responds to my queries on the topic, but at least for now, PC players of Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 2 should feel a bit safer for the time being. I'll monitor the situation and let you know of any updates as soon as I'm able. Join us on Reddit at r/WindowsCentral to share your insights and discuss our latest news, reviews, and more. ]]>
paragraphs: Classic Call of Duty games are available on Xbox backwards compatibility ... but it's a double edged sword somewhat.
For years, Modern Warfare 2 on Steam was a vector for all sorts of exploits and hacks. With this week's update, it should be solved.

Microsoft has been hard at work leveraging its Call of Duty acquisition to boost Xbox's fortunes in recent years, shipping Black Ops 1 and 2 "classic" versions exclusively onto PlayStation to huge fanfare.

Indeed, the "classic" Call of Duty versions have been in the spotlight somewhat lately, as fans clamor for an era of a more grounded, less microtransaction-laden Call of Duty. Modern versions are replete with pop culture bloat and mountains of "features" nobody really asked for, leaving nostalgic millennials and older gen-z players yearning for simpler times.

Of course, you can always play the classic Call of Duty games on PC via Steam or on Xbox Series X |S via backwards compatibility. The downside is that these classic Call of Duty versions are often infested with aimbot hackers at best, and RCE vulnerabilities at worst .

Remote Code Execution (RCE) exploits allow players in multiplayer titles to literally upload malware to your computer. The way some older games work with regard to peer-to-peer networking, if left unpatched, facilitate this malignant type of attack. Modern Warfare 2 on PC has been notorious for these types of vulnerabilities unfortunately, but there may be light at the end of the tunnel.

draft_context.source_title: macOS 26.7 Code Hints at Two Unreleased Apple Game Controllers
draft_context.description: References to two unreleased controllers that identify as Apple hardware in code were spotted in the macOS 26.7 release candidate by MacRumors reader Pdfu. Apple's first macOS 26.7 release candidate came out in mid-August, and it was full of references to unreleased Apple devices, from iPhones and Macs to new home accessories. Pdfu has continued to dig into the RC, finding new details that were previously overlooked. There are GameController profiles for two hardware devices identified as T6502 and T1057, which Pdfu suggests could be Apple gaming controllers in development. The two controllers have different haptic designs and standard controller components, like a D-pad, dual thumbsticks, shoulder buttons, Home and Menu buttons, and analog triggers. T1057 also has accelerometer and gyroscope support, while T6502 doesn't. The code includes dedicated hardware plug-ins for each device as well, which suggests these are actual devices instead of placeholder code. There have been rumors about a possible Apple game controller over the years, but nothing has ever materialized. The code found in the first macOS Tahoe 26.7 RC could point to an Apple controller in the works, but it could also be referencing internal test hardware Apple uses for testing game controller code and support. Apple removed the code in the second macOS Tahoe 26.7 RC. Apple has had multiple opportunities to release a game controller. The company could have launched one alongside any version of the Apple TV , when Apple Arcade came out, or when the Vision Pro launched, but it didn't. Instead, Apple focused on building extensive support for third-party controllers. In 2015, Apple required Apple TV games to support the Siri Remote as a gaming controller, but gave that up in a matter of months. With the Vision Pro, it partnered with Sony to add Vision Pro support to the PlayStation VR2 Sense controllers instead of designing its own controller. Console makers have mastered the controller, and many people already have Xbox, PlayStation, or Nintendo controllers. There's little improvement to be made on controller ergonomics, but if Apple is working on a controller, features like Find My and instant cross-device pairing could set it apart from competitors. All of the references can be found in blacktop/ipsw-diffs on GitHub, with Pdfu's highlights available in the forum post . article.title: ASCII smuggling isn't just an AI security risk
article.summary: Fraudsters have found a new use for ASCII smuggling, typically used to hide malicious prompts intended for AI models, in an old-school attack method: email phishing. Microsoft uncovered a massive phishing campaign using invisible Unicode tag characters that peaked at more than 2.37 million messages in late February, remained elevated during weekdays over the next three months, and gradually declined by mid-June.

draft_context.source_title: ASCII smuggling isn't just an AI security risk
draft_context.description: Fraudsters have found a new use for ASCII smuggling, typically used to hide malicious prompts intended for AI models, in an old-school attack method: email phishing. Microsoft uncovered a massive phishing campaign using invisible Unicode tag characters that peaked at more than 2.37 million messages in late February, remained elevated during weekdays over the next three months, and gradually declined by mid-June. “As AI-era attack methods become better understood, threat actors may adapt them for use in more traditional threats such as phishing and spam,” Redmond’s researchers Noam Kochavi and Sarah Wolstencroft said in a Thursday blog. “This case illustrates how techniques that emerge in AI security research can quickly cross over into established attack ecosystems, reinforcing the need for defenders to view emerging threats through a cross-domain lens.” ASCII smuggling involves using invisible or non-rendering Unicode characters to hide content inside text that appears normal to humans, and this makes it a popular technique for indirect prompt injection attacks. In these, an attacker hides instructions for an AI assistant in invisible Unicode characters, and embeds those malicious prompts inside a webpage or document. A human can’t see them, but a model can, and it decodes them as text - and may then follow the attacker’s instructions to leak data or take unauthorized actions. Instead of using ASCII smuggling for prompt injection, however, Microsoft’s security team spotted someone using invisible characters – inserting Unicode tag spaces between letters – to split financial-lure words in phishing emails in an apparent attempt to evade keyword matching and other content filters. So, for example, instead of writing “funding” in the email, the attackers wrote “fun⟨U+E0020⟩ding.” “When we looked at a sampling of the flagged messages, the surprise was there were no smuggled instructions to an AI assistant,” Kochavi and Wolstencroft wrote. “Instead, the invisible tag characters were inserted inside common financial keywords, splitting them apart so that a literal signature or keyword match would fail.” Redmond first detected the ASCII-smuggling signature in early February, flagging about 21,000 messages on February 8 before the number skyrocketed to more than 1.3 million the next day. Most of these emails came from about 150 finance-themed sender domains, and they continued for the next three months, dropping sharply after May 15 but continuing with occasional smaller spikes through at least mid-June. The security researchers pointed out two notable characteristics, including sending massive numbers of emails on weekdays and then going silent over the weekend. The campaign also had a long, gradual decline. “After an intense first phase, with weekday volumes of 1 to 2.37 million messages, peaking on February 26, the numbers stepped down slowly to roughly 80 percent less per weekday by late March.” It then dropped significantly after May 15, continuing with lower activity through mid-June. According to Redmond, the most important thing defenders can do to protect against Unicode tag blocks in phishing emails is to verify that normalization and tokenization pipelines handle tag characters consistently. “Any content that will be evaluated by keyword, signature, or regex logic should first have invisible and non-rendering Unicode code points stripped or folded, so that splicing them into a word no longer defeats the match,” the threat hunters wrote. This same control can also help reduce the threat of ASCII-smuggling against AI assistants that ingest email content. Microsoft also suggests scanning for behavioral indicators. “The observed activity had a distinctive shape: bulk volume from churning, finance-themed disposable domains, on a strict weekday-on / weekend-off schedule,” Kochavi and Wolstencroft warned. “A sudden spike of tag-block characters concentrated on finance-themed senders, switching on and off weekly, is a high-confidence campaign indicator.” ®

article.title: Anthropic lays groundwork for bots that shop for you
article.summary: Anthropic has blueprints for building e-commerce bots that shop on behalf of clients. draft_context.source_title: Anthropic lays groundwork for bots that shop for you
draft_context.description: Anthropic has blueprints for building e-commerce bots that shop on behalf of clients. That's not something many consumers want at the moment, but the AI biz this week published a set of templates for Claude-based shopping agents and merchant agents in the hope of encouraging more e-commerce businesses to implement automated purchasing. Its blueprint "contains the harnesses, patterns, and guardrails an engineering team needs to get a commerce agent running in days, with reference implementations of a shopping agent and a merchant agent for retail, travel, telecom, and ticketing platforms," the company said. Large retailers and ecommerce platforms, Anthropic observes, are using Claude to build AI agents to simplify online shopping by allowing customers to pose natural language queries to find, compare, and buy items. The buying bit may be wishful thinking: A recent Gartner survey found that while consumers use AI to find products and conduct research, they're not ready to delegate purchasing authority to AI agents. The survey found just 11 percent of consumers are willing to let AI make purchase decisions. A recent Accenture survey [PDF] is a bit more optimistic, noting, "Three in four (74 percent) consumers would let an AI agent handle routine tasks; one in three (32 percent) are ready to hand over purchase decisions; and 9 percent are open to fully autonomous shopping, before the technology is fully operational." Either way, at least AI-assisted product finding and comparison appear to be plausible activities. Anthropic's GitHub repo contains functional shopping and merchant agents that can be built with the Messages API, Agent SDK, or Claude Managed Agents. The biz's shopping agent blueprint comes with ways to connect to product catalogs, online shopping carts, checkout systems, preference databases, and purchase history databases. "A customer can say 'I need a tent, sleeping bag, and stove for a weekend trip with two kids,' and the agent can take it from there," Anthropic suggests, noting that its code supports guardrails "designed to constrain prices and products to actual catalog data, and avoids manipulative upsell patterns." Why might prices need constraint? Well, beyond the possibility of hallucinated pricing, there's considerable concern about how AI agents have the potential to compound the problems with dynamic pricing – where customers are charged different amounts for the same goods. "The rise of agentic AI, where algorithms monitor online behavior to customize costs, will likely exacerbate dynamic pricing," said the Brookings Institution earlier this year. "These agents can assess individual behavior and tailor prices based on a consumer’s shopping and purchasing history." Concerns about AI surveillance pricing were discussed last month at a Senate Judiciary subcommittee hearing. In prepared remarks, Lindsay Owens, president and CEO of Groundwork Collaborative, a Washington, DC-based advocacy group, noted that already half of those using the Walmart app use "Sparky," the company's AI assistant. Those shoppers spend about 35 percent more than those who don't, Owens said. "These agents have access to swaths of data on customers – what shoppers tell them, what they’ve purchased in the past, and in some cases, what they’ve hovered over with their mouse or even what other websites they’ve visited," she said. "All of that can be used to infer exactly how much they’re willing to pay for a product and set the price tag accordingly." Even if shoppers can be assured of getting a fair deal using AI agents, there's another concern. Monica Eaton, founder and CEO of Chargebacks911, told The Register in an emailed statement that agentic commerce looks likely to create fraud problems for merchants. There isn't yet a framework for merchants to deal with AI purchases that consumers claim they didn't authorize. "Merchants cannot become the insurer of every misunderstanding between a consumer and their AI," she said. Anthropic's templates may prove helpful for AI agent design, but the real challenge isn't technical. It's about trust – consumers have to trust that AI will act in their best interest and merchants have to trust that AI will be accountable. That may take time. ®

We've just reviewed the Google Pixel 11 Pro , and were mightily impressed by its new Magic Capture feature — but I'd still recommend picking up the Google Pixel 10 Pro this sales season, for reasons I'll explain in a moment. Magic Capture on the Pixel 11 Pro automatically takes high-quality stills while you're shooting a video. Simply press the shutter button once, hold the phone as if you’re shooting a video, and press it again when you’re finished — you'll then be presented with a regular video and photos showing key moments from the scene. In other words, this camera mode removes the need to choose whether you want photos or a video, and gives you both instead. You can see how Magic Capture plays out in the photos and video below, all of which were captured with a single tap of the shutter button when Magic Capture mode was selected: A photo captured using Magic Capture on the Pixel 11 Pro Future/Jason Cipriani A photo captured using Magic Capture on the Pixel 11 Pro Future/Jason Cipriani A photo captured using Magic Capture on the Pixel 11 Pro Future/Jason Cipriani Magic Capture is hands-down my favorite feature on the Pixel 11 Pro, and it’s something I can imagine most people making frequent use of. But despite its exclusivity to Google's new flagship, I'd still say the Google Pixel 10 Pro is the better buy this sales season — for several reasons. A cheaper choice The Pixel 10 Pro costs less, and is likely to be further reduced during sales periods (Image credit: Future) Firstly, unlike the Pixel 11 Pro — which is brand new and probably won’t be reduced for a while — the Google Pixel 10 Pro is likely to be heavily discounted for Labor Day in the US, and it’s already available at a reduced price from many retailers in the UK (it's just £649 at Amazon , for instance). That makes the 10 Pro a much better bargain than the $1,099 / £1,079 / AU$1,849 Pixel 11 Pro, especially as, even at full price, it’s still the cheaper phone (Google doubled the 11 Pro's starting storage, but kept the 10 Pro's 256GB price, effectively hiking the base cost of the Pixel 11 Pro by $100 / £80 / AU$150). And if you’re worried about missing out on things — don’t be. There’s a good chance Magic Capture itself will land on the Pixel 10 Pro and Pixel 10 Pro XL within a few months, as Google’s software features tend to trickle down to the previous generation of phones over time. That 'exclusivity' I mentioned earlier may be short-lived. Similar smartphones The Google Pixel 10 Pro has most of what the Pixel 11 Pro does (Image credit: Philip Berne / Future) And beyond Magic Capture, there’s really not that much to get excited about with the Pixel 11 Pro. HiLight under-delivers, and you actually get less RAM here, at least in the starting capacity, with the Pixel 11 Pro starting at 12GB, while the Pixel 10 Pro has 16GB in all configurations. The new phone has a slightly more powerful chipset, sure, but for the average user, the Pixel 10 Pro should deliver strong performance anyway. And there’s little difference in their respective camera hardware, batteries, or screens (other than a higher peak brightness on the new phone). So, if you’re in the US, I’d recommend keeping an eye out for Pixel 10 Pro sales this holiday season, before settling on the new model. And while the Labor Day sales won’t apply elsewhere, it’s still worth seeing if anywhere’s offering the Pixel 10 Pro at a heavily discounted price outside the US too — because if so, you should probably grab that rather than the Pixel 11 Pro. draft_context.source_title: Nvidia's RTX Spark is more impressive for gaming than I expected after going hands-on at Gamescom 2026 — but I still have one wish
draft_context.description: Gaming on the go has reached fresh heights over the years, with slim laptops and compact handhelds delivering great performance. AMD and Intel have spearheaded the charge with their mobile processors, but a new player is in town. Nvidia revealed its RTX Spark at Computex in May, an ARM-based superchip designed for Windows on ARM laptops, with AI capabilities and obvious strong suits for creators – but also gamers, too, with a powerful integrated RTX GPU. It's designed for slim laptops and compact PCs, keeping workspaces less cluttered and making creation alongside gaming much easier when travelling. I was lucky enough to go hands-on with an RTX Spark laptop at Gamescom 2026, specifically the HP OmniBook Ultra 16, which was running Borderlands 4 . Gearbox Interactive's latest entry in the franchise was notorious for its rough performance at launch . It has significantly improved since then, and the OmniBook Ultra 16 was running the game at an incredible frame rate, one I could tell was above 60 frames per second, with the help of Nvidia's Frame Generation x2. The mention of Frame Generation may throw some off; after all, it's been frowned upon for a long time with the 'fake frames' nickname (a criticism I disagree with). However, the input delay and overall latency weren't an issue for me on this RTX Spark system. (Image credit: Future) I didn't get the chance to put the system through its paces other than playing that particular game, but it's worth noting that the other RTX Spark laptops at Nvidia's booth were running games like 007 First Light and Arc Raiders , both of which ran at smooth, solid frame rates. If it wasn't clear already, I think RTX Spark is great for laptops and compact PCs, and my only concern is the price. I'm hoping for something that isn't too expensive, but that's probably wishful thinking due to the nature of these devices and the ongoing RAM crisis. However, it would be a shame if RTX Spark laptops don't blossom as a result of memory shortages. Handheld manufacturers could use RTX Spark (Image credit: Siberian Art / Shutterstock) Speaking with Nvidia's staff at Gamescom, I asked if the RTX Spark was intended to be used with handheld gaming PCs, and it was made clear that Team Green is completely open to any handheld manufacturer reaching out to use the superchip. Handheld territory isn't exactly foreign to Nvidia either. The Nintendo Switch 2 uses the Tegra T239 processor, with access to DLSS across multiple games — and the upscaling technology does wonders for image quality and performance. While AMD and Intel's processors continue to provide fantastic performance on most handheld gaming PCs, especially with Intel's new G3 Extreme CPU, I told Nvidia that DLSS on something like a Legion Go or MSI Claw would be untouchable. Of course, performance has to be balanced with battery life and power usage, as well as pricing, and I'm very aware that this could be a tricky equation to deal with. If the RTX Spark (or any similar chip in Nvidia's plans going forward) could be the engine of a handheld gaming PC, using more aggressive upscaling wouldn't be something to avoid in terms of any easy win to boost performance. DLSS Super Resolution is great at maintaining sharp image quality, and it would work even better on the smaller screen of a handheld. Will this ever happen, though? That's down to the manufacturers of these devices. ]]>

draft_context.source_title: Why is there so much worry about OpenAI Astra, and what issues could ‘recurrent depth’ reasoning cause? The experts weigh in
draft_context.description: OpenAI has unveiled a much anticipated AI model which the firm has dubbed ‘GPT-6 Astra’. While the model has improved significantly across benchmark testing and brings a host of new business features , there is still a dark cloud looming over the new model. Off the back of OpenAI’s accidental hack of Hugging Face and the company’s subsequent efforts to improve how AI agents behave and interact, numerous cybersecurity experts have raised concerns about the model’s new ‘recurrent depth’ reasoning capabilities. This new reasoning architecture allows the model to consider a problem multiple times before taking an action, compared to the standard chain-of-thought reasoning used in previous models. Why the concern about recurrent depth reasoning? This new level of reasoning apparently offers improved performance. OpenAI also says it has fixed its models' abilities to circumvent boundaries when performing tests by monitoring the models reasoning and ensuring the model stays aligned within the scope of its task. During Astra’s launch event, OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki said: “We will not accept degradation in our ability to monitor model alignment beyond a certain level. We will withhold scaling until we can regain enough confidence.” (Image credit: Future) Got an opinion for us? Here’s how you can submit your perspective But numerous experts believe that the lessons of the Hugging Face incident have not yet been learned, and the model has been released without adequate testing on Astra’s reasoning and monitoring. After all, no one thought one of OpenAI’s models could set up a hidden internet-connected messaging board that allowed AI agents to influence each other's behavior. But with Astra being released into the real world, the lessons may have to be learned on the fly. Expert perspectives on OpenAI Astra release James Blake, VP of Global Cyber Resiliency Strategy at Cohesity: The launch of Astra is raising questions again around the safety of Frontier AI. Instead of simply asking whether a model is "safe", organisations now need to ask whether it remains safe across millions of different situations, prompts and interactions. Cyber resilience has traditionally assumed that systems and threat actors behave deterministically. AI systems don’t. Suppose an AI system autonomously develops a strategy that causes financial loss, leaks confidential information or violates regulation. Who is responsible? Advanced models can and will continue to exhibit behaviours that emerge from their optimisation process rather than from explicit programming. We have to move beyond thinking about AI as just another software tool and find ways to ensure these systems remain observable, auditable and governable throughout their lifecycle. The most important question we’ll need to answer in future is one of liability. Suppose an AI system autonomously develops a strategy that causes financial loss, leaks confidential information or violates regulation. Who is responsible? The developer that trained the model? The cloud provider operating the infrastructure? Currently the answer is surprisingly unclear. It’s not just about what AI can do: it’s about who is accountable when it does something nobody expected. Oleksandr Yaremchuk, Co-Founder & CTO at Manifold Security: OpenAI is calling Astra its most aligned model yet, even as its chief scientist admits monitorability is getting harder as models get more capable. Evidently, Astra hides its reasoning in the majority of tested cases, and some successful attacks left no reasoning trace at all. That's the tool many organisations still use, including the labs themselves, for auditing what an agent is doing, and it's getting less reliable with every release. A model that explains itself less isn't more aligned, it's just harder to catch when it goes wrong. That matters because Astra isn't staying inside OpenAI's test environment. It's going to run as an agent on employee laptops and in the browser, holding real credentials, inside companies that have no way to watch what it does once it's there. A model that explains itself less isn't more aligned, it's just harder to catch when it goes wrong. Labs can keep debating what these models say or refuse to say. Security teams need to stop relying on that and start monitoring what agents actually do at runtime, with the ability to shut one down mid-action. That's the only oversight left that still works once the reasoning goes quiet. Kristin Lowery, Field CISO at Optiv: For boards and executive leaders, the emergence of OpenAI’s Astra model highlights a broader reality: AI is no longer just a productivity issue; it is a risk management issue. The real challenge is whether organizations can strengthen their governance, security controls, and workforce readiness quickly enough to keep pace Just as organizations established governance for cloud adoption and digital transformation, they now need clear policies, strong oversight, and accountability for AI use. The question is not whether AI will become more capable — it will. The real challenge is whether organizations can strengthen their governance, security controls, and workforce readiness quickly enough to keep pace. Patricia Titus, Field CISO at Abnormal AI: OpenAI crossing this threshold deserves attention. Credit where it's due, they're handling it responsibly by restricting Astra's advanced cyber capability to a small coalition rather than releasing it broadly.But this isn't one company's problem to contain. Once a model can find and exploit unknown flaws without a human in the loop, that capability doesn't stay exclusive for long. Open-weight and modified models typically trail the frontier by only months, and that's the reality defenders have to plan around now. Static, signature-based defences were built for attacks that repeat. They weren't built for an adversary that generates a new one every time. Static, signature-based defences were built for attacks that repeat. They weren't built for an adversary that generates a new one every time. Defenders need the same shift, systems that learn what normal looks like for every identity, human, machine, or AI agent, and flag and contain the moment something deviates, at machine speed. The window to build that is open now. It won't stay that way once this capability is common instead of rare. Raghu Nandakumara, VP of Industry Strategy at Illumio: With the Astra announcement, OpenAI is doubling down on monitoring the model's own behaviour – a response to the model "breakouts" seen over the past few months. The goal is to catch a model going rogue mid-task, not just stop it being misused at the outset. When Anthropic announced Claude Mythos Preview, the core concern was the model falling into the wrong hands. OpenAI's answer goes further adding guardrails around the model's own reasoning and actions, regardless of the user's intent. The goal is to catch a model going rogue mid-task, not just stop it being misused at the outset. The rest of this announcement can be summarised as ‘we have a new frontier model, and it’s more capable than the last one’. How do I submit my own perspective on emerging news? article.title: There's No Limit to How Bad Code Can Get
article.summary: It is not like a building, or a bridge, that is in the physical realm where you can see and feel the nature of the thing. If you continue to add floors and rooms to a building forever, it will collapse.
article.dek: It is not like a building, or a bridge, that is in the physical realm where you can see and feel the nature of the thing.
article.hook: It is not like a building, or a bridge, that is in the physical realm where you can see and feel the nature of the thing.

sections.heading: Context: what is changing
sections.body: Software is in the domain of the abstract. It is not like a building, or a bridge, that is in the physical realm where you can see and feel the nature of the thing. If you continue to add floors and rooms to a building forever, it will collapse. Software faces no such constraint. The code can always get worse. There can always be a new layer of indirection or a reduction in performance.

sections.heading: Where the sources line up
sections.body: Over a decade ago I had my first encounter with an ugly legacy codebase. I had just joined Amazon as a "Software Development Engineer", fresh out of university, and worked on a team that owned code related to processing orders . On the surface, what our code had to do seemed simple. Processing an order involved writing some things to a database and calling into services owned by other teams, either to ask validity questions or to update bookkeeping on their end. My colleagues and I estimated that a sufficient implementation of this system shouldn't need more than two dozen strong engineers to maintain and evolve. article.summary: Research Policy Commitments Learn News Try Claude Science Formalizing Fermat's Last Theorem Sep 4, 2026 We are sharing the first complete computer-checked proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem. Claude worked largely autonomously over 11 days to write the proof in the Lean programming language.

sections.heading: Context: what is changing
sections.body: Research Policy Commitments Learn News Try Claude Science Formalizing Fermat's Last Theorem Sep 4, 2026 We are sharing the first complete computer-checked proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem. Claude worked largely autonomously over 11 days to write the proof in the Lean programming language. Below, we describe how the formalization was done and share some thoughts about what this work could mean for research mathematics. Around 1637, Pierre de Fermat jotted down a claim in the margin of his copy of Diophantus’s Arithmetica that would become one of the most famous mathematical conjectures of all time: no positive integers a, b, c satisfy aⁿ + bⁿ = cⁿ for any n > 2. Fermat’s Last Theorem (FLT), as the conjecture became known, turned out to be incredibly difficult to prove. The first proof, from Sir Andrew Wiles in 1995, ran to 129 pages and required months of painstaking work to verify.

sections.heading: Where the sources line up
sections.body: A decade later, Dutch computer scientist Jan Bergstra proposed “formalizing” Wiles’s proof: converting the mathematical reasoning into a form computers can check automatically. Since then, mathematicians have been developing the methods needed to encode such a complex proof, including a multi-year community effort kicked off in 2024 by Kevin Buzzard at Imperial College London to complete the formalization using the Lean proof assistant .

sections.heading: Practical impact for readers
sections.body: Recently, Tianyi Peng, an Anthropic researcher whose group at Columbia University builds tools for AI formalization, set out to test whether Claude could make progress on formalizing FLT. 1 The result went further than he expected. In 11 days, working largely autonomously, Claude produced the first end-to-end, computer-checked proof of FLT. Along the way, it wrote 13 million lines of Lean and proved 29,500 intermediate theorems.

sections.heading: Who should pay attention now
sections.body: Automatically formalizing a proof as complex as FLT is a significant step towards a future in which all of mathematics can be readily checked. As AI produces ever more proofs, the ability to easily formalize work can lighten the burden of evaluating new results (a process that can take years). We are hopeful that it will become easier, not harder, to trust the body of knowledge upon which mathematics is built.
